value_domain: Australian Business Number (hashed and truncated)
value_source: Australian Business Register, ABN format
variable_description: The employer party to the apprenticeship or traineeship. An apprentice's training contract is with an employer, so this identifies who that is, and a change of value across an apprentice's records is a change of employer part-way through a training contract rather than a new apprenticeship. Because it is the same key the ATO products use, an apprenticeship can be matched to the wages the same employer reported.
description_source: Australian Business Register, ABN format
value_definition: A hash of the Australian Business Number, truncated. The Australian Business Register defines the ABN as "a unique 11 digit identifier issued to all entities registered in the Australian Business Register", structured as "a 9 digit identifier with two leading check digits" that validate on a modulus 89 calculation. Hashing replaces it with a code carrying none of those digits, so the value cannot be decoded and is useful only for matching one record to another.
limitation: The identifier stands for a registered entity, not for a workplace or a training site. Group training organisations hold the training contract while the apprentice works at a host employer, so the ABN here is often the group training organisation rather than the place of work. Truncating the hash also admits rare collisions.
rationale: The DIL gives the field as a hashed ABN on the apprentice employer table. The Australian Business Register publishes the ABN's format and issuer.
evidence_quote: The Australian Business Number (ABN) is a unique 11 digit identifier issued to all entities registered in the Australian Business Register (ABR).

value_domain: Payment group
value_source: DEWR, Australian Apprenticeship Service Delivery Operating Guidelines (Appendix E, 2024-2026 Deed RFT)
rationale: PAYMENTGROUP is the copy of the payment group carried on the payments_2023 record itself, joining to PAYMENTGROUPCODE on code_payment_type. The payment group is the higher of the two tiers in code_payment_type, with several payment types under each group. It aggregates the 2011 Census variable Labour Force Status (LFSP), which the dictionary defines as recording "for the week prior to Census Night, a person's labour force status" for persons aged 15 years and over. The family is the one the person belonged to on 2011 Census night, so this sits beside CLFEF_P_11 for employed family members and CLFUF_P_11 for unemployed ones, and the three do not add to family size.

limitation: It cannot say why anyone is outside the labour force, so a retired couple, a full-time carer and a discouraged job seeker all read the same. Because labour force status is not collected under 15, children never enter this count, and a family of two working parents with three young children scores zero here just as a childless working couple does.
rationale: The 2011 Census Dictionary defines the Labour Force Status classification this count aggregates and fixes its scope at persons aged 15 years and over, which is the fact that governs how the count behaves. A non-dependent child is a natural, adopted, step or foster child aged 15 or over who is not a full-time student aged 15 to 24 and has no partner or child of their own in the household.

value_domain: Housing utilisation on the Canadian National Occupancy Standard, 2011 Census
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2016 (cat. 2901.0), Housing Suitability (HOSD)
variable_description: Whether the person's 2011 Census dwelling had spare bedrooms or needed more, on the Canadian National Occupancy Standard. The 2016 dictionary, which first defined it, calls it "a housing utilisation measure based upon a comparison of the number of bedrooms in a dwelling together with a series of household demographics such as the number of usual residents, their relationship to one another, their age and sex". It was not a standard Census output variable in 2011, being "a new derived item for 2016", so the 2011 value in the ACLD is the same derivation applied retrospectively to 2011 records.
description_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2016 (cat. 2901.0), Housing Suitability (HOSD)
value_definition: An ordered category running from four or more extra bedrooms needed, through no bedrooms needed or spare, to four or more bedrooms spare, with codes for unable to determine, not stated and not applicable. It applies to occupied private dwellings only.
limitation: A dwelling short of bedrooms on this standard is not the same as an overcrowded one in any legal or policy sense, and the standard's assumptions about who may share a room are cultural, which the ABS has noted makes the measure a poor fit for some Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander households. The measure also takes no account of room size, dwelling condition or tenure.
rationale: The 2016 Census Dictionary entry for Housing Suitability gives the ABS definition of the housing utilisation measure and the Canadian National Occupancy Standard criteria behind it, and states that it became a standard derived item only in 2016, which is what a reader needs to interpret the ACLD's 2011 value.
evidence_quote: This is a new derived item for 2016. It is a housing utilisation measure based upon a comparison of the number of bedrooms in a dwelling together with a series of household demographics such as the number of usual residents, their relationship to one another, their age and sex.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Housing Utilisation' with the generic no-value-list sentence as both the value definition and the limitation, which left the reader with no idea that the measure compares bedrooms against a bedroom requirement, or that 2011 predates its standard release.

The standard allows no more than two people per bedroom, lets children under five of different sexes share and children under 18 of the same sex share, and gives single adults and couples a bedroom each.

rationale: The 2016 Census Dictionary entry for Housing Suitability gives the ABS definition and the Canadian National Occupancy Standard criteria for the 2016 Census; the twelve output categories are carried across from the 2021 classification, which the ABS records as unchanged since 2016.
evidence_quote: This is a new derived item for 2016. It is a housing utilisation measure based upon a comparison of the number of bedrooms in a dwelling together with a series of household demographics such as the number of usual residents, their relationship to one another, their age and sex.

It sits with CPR75D_P_11 and CPR85D_P_11, which cover 75 to 84 and 85 and over, so the three together describe the older people in the dwelling.

value_domain: Census unpaid domestic work hours band (2011)
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2011 (cat. 2901.0), Unpaid Domestic Work: Number of Hours (DOMP)
variable_description: Hours the person spent on unpaid domestic work in the week before the 2011 Census, in five broad bands. The 2011 Census Dictionary defines it as, "For each person aged 15 years and over, records the number of hours spent performing unpaid domestic work. It includes work that the person did without pay, in their own home and in other places, for themselves, their family and other people in the household, in the week prior to Census Night." The question, the reference week and the five bands are unchanged at 2016 and 2021, so DOMP_11, DOMP_16 and DOMP_21 form a comparable series.

limitation: The bands cannot be added up as hours. The top band is open, so '30 hours or more' has no ceiling and any average built from band midpoints understates the heaviest workloads. The measure also covers only the single week before Census night, so a person who was ill, travelling or on holiday that week records a figure that is not their usual pattern.
rationale: The 2011 Census Dictionary is the authority for the 2011 wave of this panel, and its DOMP entry supplies the definition, the reference week, the age scope and the exact band boundaries.
evidence_quote: For each person aged 15 years and over, records the number of hours spent performing unpaid domestic work.

value_domain: Census 2011 dwelling imputation flag (3 categories)
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2011 (cat. 2901.0), Imputation Flag for Number of Males and Females in Dwelling (IFNMFD)
variable_description: Whether the people in this person's occupied private dwelling were counted or imputed at the 2011 Census. The 2011 Census Dictionary defines the flag as one that "Indicates whether the number of males and females could be established for an occupied private dwelling, or needed to be imputed", and 2011 is the last Census with a middle category, because a collector could still obtain a count from a resident, a building manager or a neighbour when no form came back. The ACLD carries this dwelling attribute on the person record, so it describes the household the sampled person lived in rather than the answers that person gave.
description_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2011 (cat. 2901.0), Imputation Flag for Number of Males and Females in Dwelling (IFNMFD)
value_definition: Three substantive codes in the ACLD: 1 not imputed with a form returned, 2 not imputed with no form but a count obtained by the collector, and 3 imputed with neither. 98 is not applicable, covering unoccupied private dwellings, non-private dwellings and migratory, off-shore and shipping areas, and 99 marks a record not linked to the 2011 Census.
limitation: Treating code 3 as the imputation rate and comparing it with 2016 overstates the increase, because the 2016 item folds the old codes 1 and 2 into a single not-imputed category. The flag also does not say which people in the dwelling were imputed or how many, and a person imputed into a dwelling still carries values for age, sex, registered marital status and usual residence that nobody reported.
rationale: The 2011 Census Dictionary entry for IFNMFD gives the definition, the applicability and the three-way category list, and the ACLD data item list confirms the 2011 wave keeps all three categories while 2016 and 2021 keep two.
evidence_quote: Indicates whether the number of males and females could be established for an occupied private dwelling, or needed to be imputed.

variable_description: The Local Government Area of the person's usual residence at the 2021 Census, on ASGS Edition 3. The ABS defines them as follows: "Local Government Areas are an ABS Mesh Block approximation of gazetted local government boundaries as defined by each state and territory." Edition 3 has 567 Local Government Areas covering the whole of Australia, including unincorporated areas, without gaps or overlaps. The ABS warns that these "approximations of administrative boundaries do not match official legal boundaries and should only be used for statistical purposes."
description_source: ABS Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Local Government Areas

value_domain: ACLD record linkage indicator, 2011 record to 2016 Census
value_source: ABS Microdata and TableBuilder: Australian Census Longitudinal Dataset (ACLD)
variable_description: Whether the person's base Census record in this ACLD panel was linked to a 2016 Census record. It is the gate on every column ending in _16, because the ABS states that "Where records are not linked to a future Census cycle all variables for the unlinked period will be set to 'Unlinked record'." The flag exists because linkage is probabilistic, not administrative: the ABS reports that 76.0% of the 2011 panel linked forward to 2016. Filter on it before analysing any 2016 variable, or the unlinked code will be read as a real Census response.
description_source: ABS Microdata and TableBuilder: Australian Census Longitudinal Dataset (ACLD)
value_definition: A two-state indicator distinguishing records linked to the 2016 Census from records not linked. It is a linkage outcome created during ACLD construction rather than a Census response, so it has no not stated category.
limitation: A non-link is not an exit from the population. Death, emigration, a genuine Census miss and a failed match all produce the same unlinked value, so treating unlinked rows as attrition overstates mortality and emigration and understates coverage error. The flag also says nothing about the quality of the base-year record, only about the forward match.
rationale: The ABS ACLD microdata page documents the record not linked indicator and states explicitly what happens to the variables of an unlinked period, which is the fact a user of the _16 columns needs.
evidence_quote: Where records are not linked to a future Census cycle all variables for the unlinked period will be set to 'Unlinked record'.
supersedes_rationale: The entry showed only 'Record Linked Flag' with the generic no-value-list sentence as both the definition and the limitation, so nothing said which Census pair the flag covers or that unlinked rows carry a sentinel value in every 2016 column.

value_domain: ACLD record linkage indicator, base record to 2021 Census
value_source: ABS Microdata and TableBuilder: Australian Census Longitudinal Dataset (ACLD)

It governs every column ending in _21, since the ABS states that "Where records are not linked to a future Census cycle all variables for the unlinked period will be set to 'Unlinked record'." Linkage thins with distance: the ABS reports 76.0% of the 2011 panel linked to 2016 but only about 67% linked across 2011, 2016 and 2021 together. LINKFLAG_16 is the matching flag for the intermediate wave, and the two have to be read together for a three-wave analysis.
description_source: ABS Microdata and TableBuilder: Australian Census Longitudinal Dataset (ACLD)

limitation: It cannot be combined with LINKFLAG_16 to infer a person's whereabouts. Someone unlinked at 2016 but linked at 2021 was never absent from Australia; the match simply failed at one wave, so an intermittent pattern is a property of the linkage, not of the person. Nor does it indicate consent, coverage or record quality.
rationale: The ABS ACLD microdata page documents the record not linked indicators for each Census pair and the sentinel value applied to variables of an unlinked period, and the ACLD release reports the panel link rates.
evidence_quote: Where records are not linked to a future Census cycle all variables for the unlinked period will be set to 'Unlinked record'.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Record Linked Flag' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not say which wave the flag applied to, nor that it has to be used before any 2021 variable is analysed.

variable_description: The landlord of the rented dwelling the person was counted in at the 2011 Census, attached to the person's record. The 2011 Census Dictionary defines the variable as one that "Records the landlord type of rented dwellings-as classified in Tenure Type (TEND)." It applies only to occupied private dwellings being rented, including those occupied rent free, so an owner-occupier or a resident of a non-private dwelling takes a not applicable code. Housing co-operatives, community organisations and church groups had their own separate category at 2011, which later Censuses fold into community housing.

limitation: It describes a dwelling, not a person, so every ACLD member counted in the same rented dwelling carries the same value and the column cannot identify who holds the lease. Non-response was 2.3% in 2011, and a not stated value cannot be read as private rental.
rationale: The 2011 Census Dictionary entry for LLDD gives the definition, its dependence on Tenure Type and the category list in force at the Census year this column carries.
evidence_quote: Records the landlord type of rented dwellings-as classified in Tenure Type (TEND).

value_domain: asgs_mesh_block_2011
value_source: ABS ASGS 2011 Mesh Blocks (geo.abs.gov.au ASGS2011/MB), with the unlinked code from the ABS ACLD detailed microdata data item list (codeframe ACLD158)
variable_description: The Mesh Block the person was counted in on 2011 Census Night, which is place of enumeration rather than where they live. The ABS describes the unit this way: "Mesh Blocks are the smallest geographic region in the ASGS and form the basis for the larger regions of the ASGS." About 347,000 of them covered Australia in 2011. MBUCP_11 on the same row is the Mesh Block of usual residence, and the two disagree for anyone away from home that night.
description_source: Australian Bureau of Statistics, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Volume 1 - Main Structure and Greater Capital City Statistical Areas, July 2011 (cat. no. 1270.0.55.001), Mesh Blocks
value_definition: An 11-digit 2011 ASGS Mesh Block code: one digit for state or territory, then ten identifying the Mesh Block. Every larger 2011 ASGS region is built from whole Mesh Blocks, so SA1 and above can be derived from it, and 999999999999 marks an unlinked record.
limitation: It records a location on one night, not a home. A person in a hospital, a hotel, a caravan park or a prison on 9 August 2011 is coded to that Mesh Block, so an address history assembled from enumeration codes reads a night away as a move.
rationale: The ACLD workbook states the field is 11 digits against ASGS Volume 1 2011, and the ABS 2011 Mesh Block layer returns 347,519 eleven-digit codes prefixed by the state digit.
supersedes_rationale: The earlier note said no 2011 lookup exists. The bundled inst/extdata/mb_lookup.csv.gz is indeed 2021 vintage only (368,286 rows, matching the ASGS 2021 mesh block count), but the ABS publishes the 2011 mesh block list on the geo service the package already uses. Note also that MBUCD_21 and MBUCP_21 are already recorded as sourced, so the 2011 and 2016 vintages were being held to a different standard than the 2021 one.

variable_description: The Mesh Block where the person was counted on 2016 Census Night. The ABS defines the count basis as follows: "The place of enumeration is the place at which the person is counted i.e. where they spent Census Night, which may not be where they usually live." The 2016 ASGS holds 358,122 Mesh Blocks, of which 113 are non-spatial special purpose codes for Migratory - Offshore - Shipping and No usual address. MBUCP_16 gives the same person's usual residence.
description_source: Australian Bureau of Statistics, Census of Population and Housing: Understanding the Census and Census Data, Australia, 2016 (cat. no. 2900.0), Place of Enumeration vs Place of Usual Residence
value_definition: An 11-digit 2016 ASGS Mesh Block code, a state or territory digit followed by ten more. The 2016 classification is a rebuild of the 2011 one, so a code here cannot be matched to MBUCD_11 without a concordance, and 999999999999 marks an unlinked record.
limitation: A code in this column can be one of the 113 non-spatial Mesh Blocks, which means offshore, migratory or no usual address rather than a place with a boundary. Enumeration geography also carries the advantage the ABS designed it for, showing where people were on one night, which makes it the wrong basis for anything about where they live.
rationale: The ACLD workbook states the field is 11 digits against ASGS Volume 1 2016, and the ABS 2016 Mesh Block layer returns 358,009 eleven-digit codes prefixed by the state digit.
supersedes_rationale: Same as MBUCD_11: the ABS geo service publishes the 2016 mesh block list, and the 2021 equivalents of this field are already sourced.

ASGS Edition 3 has 368,286 of them covering all of Australia. value_domain: Census 2011 social marital status (MDCP) code
value_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2011, Social Marital Status (MDCP)
variable_description: The person's living arrangement at the 2011 Census: in a registered marriage, in a de facto marriage, or not married. The 2011 Census Dictionary says the variable "Reports responses to two questions: 'What is the person's relationship to Person 1/Person 2?' and 'What is the person's present marital status?'" At 2011 a person is classified as married in a registered marriage only where a husband or wife relationship answer is matched by a married response to the marital status question; a husband or wife answer with any other marital status response gives a de facto marriage. It applies only to people usually resident and present in the household on Census Night, so people in non-private dwellings are out of scope.
description_source: ABS Census Dictionary 2011, Social Marital Status (MDCP)
value_definition: One of three output categories, married in a registered marriage, married in a de facto marriage, or not married, plus not applicable. De facto covers responses reported as de facto, partner, common law husband, wife or spouse, lover, boyfriend or girlfriend.
limitation: It cannot see a partner who lives elsewhere or was away on Census Night, so a married person whose spouse was interstate is coded not married here while MSTP_11 on the same row still shows married. The registered and de facto split also turns on two answers agreeing, so a couple who called themselves husband and wife but did not report a registered marital status of married is counted here as de facto married.
rationale: The 2011 Census Dictionary entry for MDCP names the two questions it is derived from, the derivation rule in force at 2011 and the population it applies to.
evidence_quote: Reports responses to two questions: 'What is the person's relationship to Person 1/Person 2?' and 'What is the person's present marital status?'
supersedes_rationale: The entry showed 'Social Marital Status' with the generic no-value-list sentence in both fields, so it did not name the Census year, the three output categories, or the derivation rule that decides between a registered and a de facto marriage.

value_domain: Census 2016 social marital status (MDCP) code

variable_description: Whether any of the child's absence this school year was for family or cultural reasons, in the teacher's judgement. It is one of four reason items, with A1B for illness or injury, A1C for other explained reasons and A1D for unexplained reasons, all sitting beside the total band in A1.

The reason is also the teacher's attribution rather than the family's, so an absence the school never had explained to it lands in A1D instead.
rationale: The dictionary's A1a entry gives the item wording, the purpose, the two-value code frame and the 2012 revision history, which is what distinguishes it from a day count.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 no, 2 yes, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A7
variable_description: Whether the child moves around without bumping into or tripping over things, in the teacher's judgement. The instrument spells the criterion out: "Would you say this child is well co-ordinated (i.e. moves without running into or tripping over things)?". It is the gross motor counterpart to A8 and A9, which rate pen grip and object handling, and all three feed the physical health and wellbeing domain score.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A7
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for no, 2 for yes and 88 for don't know, in the same direction as A5, A6 and the B-series literacy items.
limitation: It is a single yes-or-no on whole-body movement, so it cannot grade coordination or separate a mild clumsiness from a motor impairment; the three-point items A10 and A12 are the nearest thing to a gradient. A yes also does not mean the child was assessed under comparable conditions, since teachers observe children in very different play spaces.
rationale: The dictionary's A7 entry publishes the instrument wording with its parenthetical criterion and the code frame, and section 7.1 lists A7 among the physical health and wellbeing domain items.
evidence_quote: Would you say this child is well co-ordinated (i.e. moves without running into or tripping over things)?
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Well coordinated' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without the criterion the teacher was actually asked to apply.

value_domain: AvEDI three-point proficiency rating (1 poor, 2 average, 3 good, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A8
variable_description: The teacher's rating of how well the child holds a pen, crayon or brush. The dictionary gives the purpose as "To rate how well the child holds a pen, crayon or brush", and unlike the yes-or-no items earlier in section A this one is graded on three levels. It is a fine motor item in the physical health and wellbeing domain, and the closest physical companion to the writing items B18 to B23 in the language and cognitive domain.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A8
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for poor or very poor, 2 for average, 3 for very good or good, with 88 for don't know. Both ends of the scale carry a merged label, code 1 covering poor and very poor and code 3 covering good and very good, so the extremes cannot be separated.
limitation: It cannot separate a grip problem from a lack of practice, since a child who has rarely held a pencil and a child with a motor difficulty both rate poor. The merged top and bottom categories also mean the column cannot identify the very poorest or very best writers, which matters if the intent is to find children needing occupational therapy referral.
rationale: The dictionary's A8 entry gives the instrument wording, the purpose and the three-point code frame with its merged end labels and the don't-know convention, and section 7.1 lists A8 as a physical health and wellbeing item.
evidence_quote: How would you rate this child's proficiency at holding a pen, crayon or brush
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Proficient at holding pen' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so a reader had no idea that the response is a three-point rating with merged extremes.

value_domain: AvEDI three-point proficiency rating (1 poor, 2 average, 3 good, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A9
variable_description: The teacher's rating of how well the child handles objects, on the same three-point scale as A8, A10, A11, A12 and A13. The instrument asks "How would you rate this child's ability to manipulate objects" without naming particular objects, so the teacher applies it to whatever the classroom offers. It is one of the fine motor items in the physical health and wellbeing domain.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A9
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for poor or very poor, 2 for average, 3 for very good or good, with 88 for don't know.
limitation: The question names no task, so the rating is anchored to the materials and expectations of one classroom rather than to a fixed standard, which makes it weaker for comparing individual children than for comparing large groups. It also overlaps heavily with A8, so treating the two as independent evidence of fine motor skill double counts one judgement.
rationale: The dictionary's A9 entry publishes the instrument wording, the purpose and the three-point code frame, and section 7.1 lists A9 among the physical health and wellbeing domain items.
evidence_quote: How would you rate this child's ability to manipulate objects
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Manipulates objects' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice and did not say the response is a graded rating.

value_domain: Australian Government school campus identifier
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry AGCampusID
variable_description: The Commonwealth's own code for the school campus at which the child was assessed. The dictionary defines it as "The individual campus code used by the Australian Government to identify each school campus participating in the AEDC", held on the Master Unit Record File and "Suppressed for schools outside of a data recipient's jurisdiction". It appears in PLIDA only on the 2018 cycle table, because the dictionary records the item being replaced by AGLocationID from 2021 and fully discontinued in 2024.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry AGCampusID
value_definition: A five-digit integer allocated by the Australian Government, not a serial within the AEDC file, so the value range is set by the national school register rather than by this collection.
limitation: It cannot follow a school across cycles in PLIDA, since only the 2018 table carries it and its successors sit under different names; SCHOOLID is the identifier present in every cycle. It also identifies a campus, not a school or a teacher, so a multi-campus school splits across values while TEACHERID separates classes within a campus.
rationale: The dictionary's AGCampusID entry gives the definition, the five-digit format, the Master URF availability, the jurisdictional suppression rule and the 2021 replacement and 2024 discontinuation, which together explain why it appears in one PLIDA cycle only.
evidence_quote: The individual campus code used by the Australian Government to identify each school campus participating in the AEDC.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's 'National campus identifier used by deewr' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and gave no hint that the identifier is suppressed outside a recipient's jurisdiction or that it lives on only one cycle.

value_domain: AEDC narrow age band (16 categories)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry AgeCat
variable_description: The finest published banding of the child's age, in steps of roughly three months across the school-entry range. It is a derived variable, built from the age the dictionary describes as "based on the student's reported date of birth and the date on which the Instrument was completed by the teacher". AGECUT, AGEGROUP and AGEGROUP3TO7 on the same row are coarser cuts of the same underlying age, and AGEINMONTHS is the ungrouped version.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry AgeCat
value_definition: A two-digit integer from 0 to 15, so sixteen codes despite the name; the '15 narrow' in the custodian's label counts the non-zero codes. Codes 1 to 13 step in roughly three-month intervals from 3 years 8 months to 6 years 10 months; code 0 is everything under 3 years 8 months, code 14 spans 6 years 10 months to 7 years 6 months, and code 15 is everything above.
limitation: The bands are not equal width, so treating the code as a linear age scale compresses the middle and stretches both tails, and a regression on the raw code will not recover a per-month effect. Age is also measured at the day the teacher completed the instrument rather than at a fixed census date, so two children on the same code were assessed at different points in the school year.
rationale: The dictionary's AgeCat entry publishes all sixteen bands with their exact year-and-month boundaries and marks the variable as derived, and section 4.4 states how AEDC age is constructed.
evidence_quote: AEDC age is based on the student's reported date of birth and the date on which the Instrument was completed by the teacher.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Age categories (15 narrow)' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, giving neither the number of codes nor the fact that the bands are uneven at both ends.

value_domain: AEDC broad age band (three categories)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry AgeCut
variable_description: The coarsest numeric grouping of the child's age, splitting the cohort into under five, five, and six or older. The dictionary marks it as derived and gives its purpose as "A grouping variable for child age", which is what it is normally used for: a control or a cross-tabulation axis when the sixteen bands of AGECAT are too fine. AGEGROUP holds the same idea as text with the top group cut at seven rather than six.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry AgeCut
value_definition: A single-digit integer with three codes: 0 for under 5 years, 1 for 5 years and 2 for 6 years and older.
limitation: Its top and bottom categories are open, so a four-year-old and a three-year-old share code 0 while a six-year-old and an eight-year-old share code 2, which hides exactly the age spread that matters when comparing schools with different entry rules. The bottom category also mixes children the AEDC excludes from domain categories, those under four years, with four-year-olds who are scored.
rationale: The dictionary's AgeCut entry gives the purpose, the derived source and the three-code frame, and section 3.1 records that domain categories are not calculated for children less than four years of age.
evidence_quote: Domain indicator categories are not calculated for children diagnosed with special needs, or children less than four years of age.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Age categories (3 broad)' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without the cut points or the interaction with the under-four exclusion.

value_domain: AEDC confidentialised age group (text)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry AgeGroup
variable_description: The confidentialised age grouping the AEDC uses in its published outputs, held as text rather than as a code. Section 4.4 of the dictionary says the age variable is "available in years and is confidentialised as follows" and then lists under five years, five years, six years and over six years, and this is the column that carries that grouping. AGECUT expresses almost the same split numerically, but its top band starts at six while this one holds six-year-olds separately and reserves its top value for seven and over.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry AgeGroup
value_definition: A two-character text field with four values: '<5' for under 5 years, '5' for 5 to under 6, '6' for 6 to under 7, and '>6' for 7 years and over. The field is left justified, not numeric.
limitation: Two of its four values are not numbers, so converting the column to numeric silently drops the youngest and oldest children to missing and leaves an apparently clean five-and-six-year-old sample that is missing its tails. The label '>6' is also misleading on its own, since the dictionary defines it as age 7 years or more rather than anything above six.
rationale: The dictionary's AgeGroup entry gives the four text values with their exact age boundaries and records the field as text with left justification, and section 4.4 states the confidentialisation rule the grouping implements.
evidence_quote: This variable is available in years and is confidentialised as follows:
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Age group' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and did not warn that the column is text or that '>6' means seven and over.

value_domain: AEDC age in completed years, top coded at 7
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry AgeGroup3to7
variable_description: The child's age in completed years at the time the teacher filled in the instrument, held as a plain integer from 3 to 7. It is the numeric age variable most convenient for analysis on the AEDC core tables, and the dictionary marks it as derived rather than reported. AGEINMONTHS is the finer version of the same quantity, AGECAT the finer banding, and AGEGROUP the text grouping used for publication.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry AgeGroup3to7
value_definition: A single-digit integer taking 3 for age 3 to under 4, 4 for 4 to under 5, 5 for 5 to under 6, 6 for 6 to under 7, and 7 for 7 and over. Only the top code is open; the others are exact one-year intervals.
limitation: Its name suggests a range of three to seven, but code 7 is a top code with no upper bound, so an eight-year-old repeating a year is indistinguishable from a child who has just turned seven. Rounding down to completed years also loses up to eleven months of development, which is large relative to the age effects the AEDC domain cut-offs are designed to absorb.
rationale: The dictionary's AgeGroup3to7 entry publishes the five codes with their exact age intervals and marks the source as derived, and section 4.4 states that AEDC age is built from date of birth against the instrument completion date.
evidence_quote: Age >= 7
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's 'Age in years' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it never said that 7 is a top code rather than an exact age.

value_domain: Age in completed months
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry AgeInMonths
variable_description: The child's age in whole months when the teacher completed the instrument, and the finest age measure on the AEDC file. The dictionary marks it as derived and section 4.4 explains the derivation: "AEDC age is based on the student's reported date of birth and the date on which the Instrument was completed by the teacher." Every other age column on the row, AGECAT, AGECUT, AGEGROUP and AGEGROUP3TO7, is a banding of this quantity.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry AgeInMonths
value_definition: A three-digit integer counting completed months, so a child of five years and three months is 63. There is no code frame; the domain is open across the school-entry age range.
limitation: It is age at assessment, not age at a common reference date, so it moves with when in the school year the teacher happened to complete the instrument as much as with the child's date of birth; MOC, the month of completion, is the column needed to adjust for that. It also cannot be turned back into a date of birth, which is not released.
rationale: The dictionary's AgeInMonths entry gives the derived source and the three-digit integer format, and section 4.4 states the derivation from reported date of birth against the instrument completion date.
evidence_quote: AEDC age is based on the student's reported date of birth and the date on which the Instrument was completed by the teacher.
supersedes_rationale: The entry restated 'Age in months' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without saying what the age is measured against, which is the whole difficulty with the column.

value_domain: Year of first arrival in Australia (four-digit year, 9999 unknown)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry ArrivalYear
variable_description: The year the child first came to Australia, asked on the instrument as "In which year did the child first arrive in Australia". Read against AGEINMONTHS it gives an approximate age at migration, and against COUNTRY and PLACEOFBIRTH on the same row it distinguishes a child born overseas who arrived as an infant from one who arrived shortly before starting school. The dictionary records the item as introduced in 2015, which is why it is absent from the 2009 and 2012 cycle tables.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry ArrivalYear
value_definition: A four-digit integer holding a calendar year, with 9999 reserved for unknown. There is no separate not-applicable code for children born in Australia.
limitation: The 9999 sentinel is a valid four-digit year to any arithmetic, so a mean or a difference computed without excluding it is badly wrong. It also records the first arrival, so a child who left and returned is dated by the earlier trip, and it says nothing about visa status or whether the family arrived together.
rationale: The dictionary's ArrivalYear entry gives the definition, the instrument wording, the four-digit format with 9999 for unknown, and the 2015 introduction, matching the cycles on which the column appears in PLIDA.
evidence_quote: In which year did the child first arrive in Australia
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Year of arrival' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and did not disclose the 9999 sentinel, which is the practical trap in the column.

value_domain: Indigenous status (Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander origin)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry ATSI
variable_description: Whether the child is recorded as being of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin, the gate on every other item in the AEDC Indigenous table. The dictionary defines it as follows: "A child is considered to be 'Indigenous' if he or she identifies as being of Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander origin. The term 'origin' is considered to relate to people's Australian Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander descent and for some, but not all, their cultural identity." ATSITYPE beside it splits Aboriginal from Torres Strait Islander origin, and B1A to B1D rate the child's use of Aboriginal English, Kriol and traditional languages.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry ATSI
value_definition: A single-digit integer, documented by the AEDC as 0 for no and 1 for yes. The PLIDA data item list describes the field differently, as 1 for Indigenous with null signifying non-Indigenous or non-identifying, so the negative case may arrive as missing rather than as zero.
limitation: The two published descriptions disagree on how a non-Indigenous child is stored, so a test written as ATSI equals 0 can return nobody while ATSI equals 1 works; check the observed values before building a denominator. The item is also a school enrolment record of origin rather than a self-report by the child or family at census time, and 'not identifying' is indistinguishable from 'not Indigenous' in either coding.
rationale: The dictionary's ATSI entry carries the full origin definition, the instrument wording and the two-value code frame, and the PLIDA data item list for the same column states a different missing convention, which is the discrepancy a user has to resolve.
evidence_quote: A child is considered to be 'Indigenous' if he or she identifies as being of Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander origin.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried only the PLIDA wording about nulls and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without the AEDC's own definition of origin or any note that the two sources describe the coding differently.

value_domain: Indigenous origin type (Aboriginal, Torres Strait Islander, both, neither, not stated)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry ATSIType
variable_description: Which Indigenous origin the child is recorded as having, asked only where ATSI on the same row is yes. The dictionary states the filter as "Only answer if ATSI = Yes" and the jurisdictional rule as "Not provided in New South Wales", with a 2015 filter revision noting that previous cycles did not include NSW students at all. Its purpose is to add detail rather than to change the count of Indigenous children, which ATSI alone establishes.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry ATSIType
value_definition: A single-digit integer with five codes: 1 Aboriginal but not Torres Strait Islander origin, 2 Torres Strait Islander but not Aboriginal origin, 3 both, 4 neither, and 9 not stated or unknown. The 2012 cycle revised these field values.
limitation: Its blanks are dominated by the filter and by New South Wales, so a national split of Aboriginal against Torres Strait Islander children taken from this column omits the largest jurisdiction and is not comparable across cycles. Code 4, neither origin, can also appear on rows where ATSI is yes, so the two columns can contradict each other and ATSI should be the one used to define the population.
rationale: The dictionary's ATSIType entry gives the purpose, the instrument wording, the five-code frame, the conditional filter on ATSI, the New South Wales exclusion and the 2012 and 2015 revisions.
evidence_quote: Only answer if ATSI = Yes
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Indigenous background' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and never disclosed the filter, the New South Wales gap or the internally contradictory 'neither' code.

value_domain: AvEDI three-point proficiency rating with not-applicable (1 poor, 2 average, 3 good, 88, 99)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B1
variable_description: The teacher's rating of how effectively the child uses English, asked as "How would you rate this child's ability to use language effectively in English". The dictionary allocates it to the communication skills and general knowledge domain, not to language and cognitive skills, so it feeds COMGEN rather than LANGCOG. B1A to B1D in the AEDC Indigenous table carry the parallel ratings for Aboriginal English, Kriol, traditional languages and other Indigenous languages, and ESL and LANG on the core table record whether English is the home language at all.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B1
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for poor or very poor, 2 for average, 3 for very good or good, with 88 for don't know and 99 for not applicable. It is one of the few AvEDI items to carry the not-applicable code.
limitation: A low rating is not evidence of a language delay: the item rates English specifically, so a child fluent in another language and new to English scores at the bottom on linguistic competence they in fact have. Reading it alongside LBOTE, ESL and the B1A to B1D Indigenous language ratings is the only way to tell the two situations apart.
rationale: The dictionary's B1 entry gives the instrument wording and the five-value code frame, section 7.1 lists B1 under the communication skills and general knowledge domain, and the B1a entry establishes the parallel other-language items.
evidence_quote: How would you rate this child's ability to use language effectively in English
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Proficient in english' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and did not say which domain the item feeds or that a low score can reflect language background rather than ability.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 no, 2 yes, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B10
variable_description: Whether the child shows curiosity about printed material, asked as "Would you say this child is interested in reading (inquisitive/curious about the meaning of printed material)?". It is one of the twenty-six items, B8 to B33, that the dictionary allocates to the language and cognitive skills domain, and it sits at the disposition end of that set: B11 to B17 test what the child can actually do with letters and words. E7 on the core table records whether the child is read to at home.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B10
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for no, 2 for yes and 88 for don't know, so the higher code is the positive answer across the whole B10 to B19 block.
limitation: It rates an attitude the teacher infers from behaviour in class, so a child who is interested in books at home but reticent at school reads as a no; it is not a measure of reading ability, which B15 to B17 carry. The binary form also gives no gradient, so it cannot separate mild from strong interest.
rationale: The dictionary's B10 entry gives the instrument wording with its parenthetical criterion and the code frame, and section 7.1 lists B10 among the language and cognitive skills domain items.
evidence_quote: Would you say this child is interested in reading (inquisitive/curious about the meaning of printed material)?
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Interested in reading' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, giving neither the code direction nor the distinction from the reading skill items.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 no, 2 yes, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B11
variable_description: Whether the child can name at least some letters of the alphabet, the first rung of the literacy ladder in the AvEDI. The instrument asks "Would you say this child is able to identify some letters of the alphabet", with no threshold on how many. It is a language and cognitive skills domain item and the base for B12, which asks whether the child can attach sounds to letters.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B11
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for no, 2 for yes and 88 for don't know.
limitation: Because 'some' is undefined, the item saturates: most children in their first year of school answer yes, so it separates the very lowest group from everyone else and carries almost no information about the rest. It also does not distinguish recognising a letter shape from knowing its name or its sound.
rationale: The dictionary's B11 entry gives the instrument wording, which sets the threshold at 'some letters', along with the code frame, and section 7.1 lists B11 among the language and cognitive skills domain items.
evidence_quote: Would you say this child is able to identify some letters of the alphabet
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Identifies letters' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and did not convey how low the threshold is.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 no, 2 yes, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B12
variable_description: Whether the child can attach sounds to letters, the phonics step between recognising letters in B11 and reading words in B15. The dictionary gives its purpose as "To identify if the child is able to attach sounds to letters", asked of the teacher as a single yes-or-no judgement. It is one of the language and cognitive skills domain items and, with B13 on rhyming, one of the two phonological awareness questions in the instrument.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B12
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for no, 2 for yes and 88 for don't know.
limitation: It is the teacher's impression from ordinary classroom work rather than a phonics assessment, so it will track how much explicit phonics teaching the class has done as well as the child's own skill. Nothing in the column says how many letter-sound correspondences the child knows, so it cannot be used to rank children within the yes group.
rationale: The dictionary's B12 entry gives the data element description, the purpose, the instrument wording and the code frame, and section 7.1 lists B12 among the language and cognitive skills domain items.
evidence_quote: Would you say this child is able to attach sounds to letters
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Sounds to letters' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, with no code frame and no placement in the literacy sequence.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 no, 2 yes, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B13
variable_description: Whether the child notices that words rhyme, asked as "Would you say this child is showing awareness of rhyming words". Rhyme awareness is the oral side of early literacy, so this item and B12 on letter sounds are the two phonological questions in a block otherwise concerned with print. It counts towards the language and cognitive skills domain score.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B13
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for no, 2 for yes and 88 for don't know.
limitation: Rhyme is language specific, so a child whose home language is not English can show the awareness in that language and still be rated no here, which is why B1, LBOTE and ESL belong in any interpretation of a low score. The wording asks only whether awareness is showing, not whether the child can produce rhymes, so a yes sets a low bar.
rationale: The dictionary's B13 entry gives the description, purpose, instrument wording and code frame, and section 7.1 lists B13 among the language and cognitive skills domain items alongside the print-based items.
evidence_quote: Would you say this child is showing awareness of rhyming words
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Rhyming awareness' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and gave no sense of how the item behaves for children who speak another language at home.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 no, 2 yes, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B14
variable_description: Whether the child can take part in group reading activities, the only item in the literacy block that is about behaviour in a group rather than an individual skill. The dictionary's purpose is "To identify if the child is able to participate in group reading activities". It counts towards the language and cognitive skills domain, but what it measures overlaps with the classroom conduct items in section C, since sitting through a shared book requires attention as much as reading.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B14
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for no, 2 for yes and 88 for don't know.
limitation: It depends on the classroom running group reading at all, so a no can mean the activity does not happen rather than that the child cannot join in, and the don't-know code is the only place that shows. It also confounds reading with attention and social participation, so it should not be read as evidence about reading skill on its own.
rationale: The dictionary's B14 entry gives the description, purpose, instrument wording and code frame, and section 7.1 places B14 in the language and cognitive skills domain while the attention and conduct items sit in the social competence and emotional maturity domains.
evidence_quote: Would you say this child is able to participate in group reading activities
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Group reading' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and did not flag that the item is conditional on classroom practice.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 no, 2 yes, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B15
variable_description: Whether the child can read simple words, the first of three items that step up in difficulty through B16 for complex words and B17 for simple sentences. The instrument asks "Would you say this child is able to read simple words", leaving 'simple' to the teacher's judgement. All three are language and cognitive skills domain items, and together they are the part of the AvEDI that discriminates among the more advanced readers at school entry.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B15
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for no, 2 for yes and 88 for don't know.
limitation: The instrument does not enforce the ladder, so a child can be coded no here and yes on B16 or B17; the three items are not a scale and should not be summed without checking for those inconsistent patterns. value_domain: AEDC domain score, 0 to 10
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary (Version 7.0, February 2025), Australian Government Department of Education, section 3.1 and data element COMGEN
variable_description: The child's score on communication skills and general knowledge, one of the five AEDC developmental domains. It is derived from the teacher's answers to the domain's instrument items rather than reported directly, and the AEDC calculates it only "provided that each child has 75 per cent or more of these items completed". Three columns beside it do the interpreting: COMGENVALID says whether the score may be used, COMGENCATEGORY places it in the vulnerable, at risk and on track bands, and COMGEN_1 is the single sub-domain sitting underneath it.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary (Version 7.0, February 2025), Australian Government Department of Education, section 3.1 and data element COMGEN
value_definition: A numeric field carried to four decimal places, on a scale where "children receive a score between zero and ten, where higher scores denote higher levels of development". There is no code list; the domain is the continuous range.
limitation: It is not an individual diagnosis. The AEDC states that its indicators "have been developed and validated for use as a population measure at a group level and have not been psychometrically tested for application in relation to individual children", so a low score for one child carries far less meaning than a low share across a community. The scoring method is licensed from McMaster University and is not published, so the number cannot be recomputed or audited from the item responses held in the same file.
rationale: Section 3.1 of the Data Dictionary sets out the domain scoring rule, the zero-to-ten scale and the 75 per cent completion threshold, and the COMGEN element page gives the 7.4 numeric field format and the derived source.
evidence_quote: For each of the five AEDC domains, children receive a score between zero and ten, where higher scores denote higher levels of development.
supersedes_rationale: The entry showed the custodian's wording, 'Communication and general knowledge', and the generic no-value-list sentence as both the value definition and the limitation, which left the reader with no scale, no direction and no idea that the score is a group-level measure.

value_domain: aedc_edi_score_0_10 (numeric, 0 to 10 inclusive, 4 decimal places; higher = higher development)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary (Version 7.0, February 2025), Australian Government Department of Education (sections 3.1, 15, 16) and AEDC Data Guidelines 2025, Australian Government Department of Education
variable_description: The child's sub-domain score for communication skills and general knowledge, derived from the teacher's answers on the instrument. The 2025 AEDC Data Dictionary records the element as "Communication skills and general knowledge" and its purpose as determining the child's communication skills and general knowledge. Communication skills and general knowledge is the one AEDC domain with a single sub-domain, so this column sits directly under the domain score of the same name.
description_source: Australian Government Department of Education, AEDC Data Dictionary (Version 7.0, February 2025), sections 3.1 and 16
value_definition: A number held in a 7.4 field, so up to four decimal places, on the AEDC scale where "children receive a score between zero and ten, where higher scores denote higher levels of development". Domain scores are only calculated when at least 75 per cent of the underlying items were completed.
limitation: The AEDC states that sub-domain data "is only made available for exploratory research purposes" while its validity is still under investigation, so it does not carry the standing of the five domain scores. It is also a bare score with no cut-off attached: the vulnerable, at risk and on track categories are defined for domains, not for this column.
rationale: The Communication skills and general knowledge sub-domain score is stored in the same numeric 7.4 field as the five AEDC domain scores, and the AEDC publishes the domain-score scale as zero to ten; the sub-domain scale is inferred to be the same, but the AEDC never states it for sub-domains.
evidence_quote: children receive a score between zero and ten
supersedes_rationale: The earlier review needed the licensed McMaster scoring formula. The formula stays proprietary, but the scale the score sits on is documented and is enough to give the column a defensible domain.

value_domain: AEDC domain vulnerability category
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary (Version 7.0, February 2025), Australian Government Department of Education, section 3.1 and data element COMGENCategory
variable_description: Where the child's communication and general knowledge score falls in the national score distribution, banded into four percentile groups. Code 1 is the 0 to 10th percentile, which is what the AEDC reports as developmentally vulnerable on this domain, and it is the column most published AEDC vulnerability figures for communication are built from. The cut-offs are fixed at the 2009 baseline: the dictionary records that "the cut-off scores used in 2009 have remained the same across each collection cycle", so a rise in the share coded 1 is a real fall in scores rather than a moving benchmark.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary (Version 7.0, February 2025), Australian Government Department of Education, section 3.1 and data element COMGENCategory
value_definition: A one-digit integer with four bands: 1 = 0 to 10th percentile, 2 = 11th to 25th, 3 = 26th to 50th, 4 = 51st to 100th. The percentiles are those of the 2009 national distribution, not of the child's own cycle.
limitation: It is not calculated for every child. rationale: The COMGENCategory element page publishes the four percentile bands verbatim, and section 3.1 states the 2009 baseline rule and the exclusions applied to the domain categories.
evidence_quote: Domain indicator categories are not calculated for children diagnosed with special needs, or children less than four years of age.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Vulnerable - communication' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it neither named the four bands nor said that vulnerability means the bottom decile of a fixed 2009 distribution.

value_domain: AEDC domain validity flag
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary (Version 7.0, February 2025), Australian Government Department of Education, data element COMGENValid
variable_description: Whether the child's communication and general knowledge score may be used, and the gate the AEDC applies before reporting COMGEN or COMGENCATEGORY. The dictionary sets 0 to mean the "Child has special needs status, is 3 years old or has too many unanswered instrument questions for the domain" and 1 to mean the child meets all three conditions, so a score can exist in the file and still be flagged out of scope. PHYSVALID, SOCVALID, EMOTVALID and LANGCOGVALID apply the identical test to the other four domains, and VALIDDOMAINS counts how many of the five a child has a valid score for.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary (Version 7.0, February 2025), Australian Government Department of Education, data element COMGENValid
value_definition: A one-digit integer: 0 not valid for reporting, 1 valid. The two labels are the same wording used on every AEDC domain validity flag.
limitation: It does not say which of the three reasons applies. Anyone who wants to keep children with special needs but drop those with too few completed items has to rebuild the test from SPECIALNEEDS, the age columns and the instrument item responses, because this single code cannot separate an excluded three-year-old from a child whose teacher left half the domain blank.
rationale: The COMGENValid element page publishes both field values with their full labels, and the same labels recur on the four sibling domain validity flags, confirming the pattern.
evidence_quote: Child has special needs status, is 3 years old or has too many unanswered instrument questions for the domain
supersedes_rationale: The entry gave 'Valid - communication and general knowledge' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, hiding the fact that the flag collapses three different exclusions into one code.

value_domain: AEDC cultural consultant assistance flag
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary (Version 7.0, February 2025), Australian Government Department of Education, data element Consult
variable_description: Whether an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Cultural Consultant helped the teacher complete the instrument for this child. evidence_quote: Is your completion of the AvEDI being assisted by discussion with an Indigenous Consultant

value_domain: AEDC vulnerability summary indicator
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary 2025, item DV1 and section 3.2 Summary Indicators
variable_description: Whether the child was developmentally vulnerable on one or more of the five AEDC domains, the headline AEDC result. The dictionary describes it as "Vulnerable - One or more domains" and notes that "Vulnerability Summary Indicators do not have a score or cut-off scores as they are calculated from the number of domains a child is vulnerable on", so it is derived from PHYSCATEGORY, SOCCATEGORY, EMOTCATEGORY, LANGCOGCATEGORY and COMGENCATEGORY beside it. Vulnerable means a domain category of 1, the 0 to 10th percentile band, cut against the 2009 baseline that is held fixed for every later cycle so that cycles can be compared.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary 2025, item DV1 and section 3.2 Summary Indicators
value_definition: A one-digit integer taking 0 or 1. There is no not-applicable code, so DV1FLAG beside it is what tells you whether a 0 is a real result.
limitation: A 0 does not mean the child was assessed and found not vulnerable. The dictionary states that domain indicator categories are not calculated for children with special needs status or children under four years of age, and those children still appear with DV1 of 0, so any rate computed over all rows is wrong. DV1 also says nothing about which domain or how far below the cut-off the child fell; LOWTOTAL and the five category columns carry that.
rationale: The dictionary defines the element, explains in section 3.2 how the summary indicators are built from the domain categories, and states the exclusions that make the raw column unsafe to average.
evidence_quote: Domain indicator categories are not calculated for children diagnosed with special needs, or children less than four years of age.
supersedes_rationale: The entry showed 'Vulnerable - one or more domains' with the generic no-value-list sentence printed twice, giving no warning that the zeros include children who were never scored and no pointer to the denominator flag next to it.

value_domain: AEDC summary indicator denominator flag
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary 2025, item DV1Flag and Appendix 3 section A2.1.1
variable_description: Whether the child belongs in the denominator when a developmentally-vulnerable-on-one-or-more rate is calculated. The dictionary defines it as "Qualifies for the denominator of DV1" and explains that the flag exists because, when the Canadian Early Development Instrument was adapted for Australia, "work was conducted to refine the denominator (i.e., valid cases) for these two indicators to maximise the number of cases with reportable data". A published AEDC rate is therefore the count of DV1 equal to 1 over the count of DV1FLAG equal to 1, not over every row in the file.
description_source: AEDC Data Dictionary 2025, item DV1Flag and Appendix 3 section A2.1.1
value_definition: A one-digit integer taking 0 or 1, where 1 means the child's record supports a DV1 result.
limitation: It is not a quality flag for the record as a whole. A child excluded here can still have valid age, language, schooling and special needs entries, and DV2FLAG and OT5FLAG in the same table carry their own denominators, so the three summary indicators are not computed over identical populations and their rates cannot be differenced as if they were.
rationale: The dictionary gives the element entry and Appendix 3 explains why the flag was created and what refining the denominator was for, which is the fact that makes the column usable.
evidence_quote: Two new variables, DV1Flag and DV2Flag, were created in the dataset to define this information.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Qualifies for the denominator of dv1' with the generic no-value-list sentence as both value definition and limitation, so it never said how to use the flag or that the other summary indicators have different denominators.

variable_description: Whether the child fell in the lowest AEDC category on at least two of the five developmental domains, the headline measure the AEDC reports as developmentally vulnerable on two or more domains. It is built by counting how many of PHYSCATEGORY, SOCCATEGORY, EMOTCATEGORY, LANGCOGCATEGORY and COMGENCATEGORY equal 1, the 0 to 10th percentile band of the 2009 national baseline. The dictionary notes that summary indicators "do not have a score or cut-off scores as they are calculated from the number of domains a child is vulnerable on".
