value_domain: ASGS 2021 Statistical Area Level 2 code
value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Statistical Area Level 2
variable_description: The 2021-vintage SA2 the DSS geocoder assigned to the address, for the client on special_client and for the outlet on special_outlet. It is the level most analyses of Data Exchange geography settle on, because it is fine enough to be locally meaningful and coarse enough to publish without identifying a provider or a client. Where the analysis needs the outlet's ABS-derived geography instead, SA2_ASGS_2021 on the outlet table is the equivalent column.
description_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Statistical Area Level 2
value_definition: A 9-digit hierarchical code under ASGS Edition 3, July 2021 to June 2026. There are 2,473 SA2s, including 19 non-spatial special purpose codes for populations that cannot be placed, such as No Usual Address.
limitation: For a client this is the geography of the address on file, which the protocols allow to be a substitute: a homeless client's record may hold the suburb where they usually sleep or the suburb of the outlet, and a client at risk of family violence may have the outlet's address recorded instead of their own. Reading client SA2 counts as a map of where clients live therefore pulls people towards the suburbs where services sit.
rationale: ABS publishes the SA2 definition, count and coding structure for the edition named in the column, and the protocols state the address substitutions permitted for homeless and at-risk clients that determine what the client-side code actually describes.
evidence_quote: There are 2,473 SA2s covering the whole of Australia without gaps or overlaps.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried source-defined values with the boilerplate definition and the generic 'The source defines the value domain' limitation, and its description was the custodian's wording about boundary tagging.

value_domain: ASGS 2016 Statistical Area Level 3 code
value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS): Volume 1 - Main Structure and Greater Capital City Statistical Areas, July 2016
variable_description: The 2016-vintage SA3 the DSS geocoder assigned to the address on the client or outlet record. SA3s group SA2s into regions of roughly 30,000 to 130,000 people, which is the scale at which service coverage across a district can be described without exposing an individual provider. Note the asymmetry on special_outlet: it carries SA3 boundary codes from the DSS geocoder, but the ABS-coded block on that table has no SA3 column, running from SA2_ASGS_2021 straight to SA4_ASGS_2021.
description_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS): Volume 1 - Main Structure and Greater Capital City Statistical Areas, July 2016
value_definition: A 5-digit hierarchical code on the ASGS July 2016 edition: one digit for state or territory, two for SA4 and two for the SA3 within it. It is also the first five digits of the SA1 and SA2 codes on the same row.
limitation: SA3s are drawn for regional statistical output and deliberately ignore local government and service catchment boundaries, so an SA3 tally will not match a council's own figures or a program's funded region. The 2016 and 2021 SA3 sets differ in both number and shape, so the two boundary code columns cannot be pooled.
rationale: ABS published the SA3 structure and coding for the July 2016 edition the column is named after, and the registry's table layout shows which levels the DSS geocoder supplies against which levels ABS supplies on special_outlet.
evidence_quote: Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS): Volume 1 - Main Structure and Greater Capital City Statistical Areas, July 2016
supersedes_rationale: The domain was 'not specified' and the generic no-value-list sentence was printed twice, so the page could not even say the code was five digits.

value_domain: ASGS 2021 Statistical Area Level 3 code
value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Statistical Area Level 3
variable_description: The 2021-vintage SA3 the DSS geocoder assigned to the address, on both the client and the outlet records. It is the middle rung of the boundary code family, the level at which many DSS program reports are published because it survives disclosure control while still describing a recognisable district. There is no ABS-coded SA3 column in this product, so this is the only SA3 available for the 2021 vintage.
description_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Statistical Area Level 3
value_definition: A 5-digit hierarchical code under ASGS Edition 3: one digit for state or territory, two for SA4 and two for the SA3. There are 359 SA3s, including 19 non-spatial special purpose codes.
limitation: An SA3 is large enough that services anywhere across a whole city fringe look identical, so using it as the analytical unit throws away the SA1 and SA2 detail on the same row for no gain unless disclosure requires it. It is also not a program boundary: DSS funded activity regions and SA3s do not align.
rationale: ABS publishes the SA3 definition, count and coding structure for the edition the column is named after, and the registry shows the column is one of the DSS-geocoded boundary set rather than the ABS-coded ASGS block.
evidence_quote: There are 359 SA3s covering the whole of Australia without gaps or overlaps.
supersedes_rationale: The domain was 'not specified', and the value definition and the limitation were the same generic sentence about no finite value list.

value_domain: ASGS 2021 Statistical Area Level 4 code
value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Statistical Area Level 4
variable_description: The SA4 the service outlet sits in, coded by ABS from the address register match, and the coarsest sub-state level in the ABS block on this table. ABS describes SA4s as "geographic areas built from whole Statistical Areas Level 3 (SA3s)" that are "the largest sub-state regions in the Main Structure of the ASGS", with boundaries drawn to represent labour markets. Because Labour Force estimates are published at SA4, this is the column that lets outlet activity be read against regional unemployment and participation.
description_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Statistical Area Level 4
value_definition: A 3-digit code: a one-digit state or territory identifier followed by a two-digit SA4 identifier unique within that state, as in 102 for Central Coast. There are 108 SA4s under ASGS Edition 3, including 19 non-spatial special purpose codes, and the four Other Territories share a single SA4.
limitation: SA4s hold between 100,000 and 500,000 people and exist to support Labour Force sampling, not service planning, so they are far too coarse to show where a service is needed. The count also changed between editions, from 107 in the 2016 ASGS to 108 in Edition 3, so a series that crosses the change needs a concordance rather than a direct join.
rationale: ABS publishes the SA4 definition, purpose, count and coding structure for the edition named in the column, and DSS's own registry gives the 2016 SA4 count as 107, which fixes the discontinuity between the two vintages.
evidence_quote: Statistical Area Level 4 (SA4s) are geographic areas built from whole Statistical Areas Level 3 (SA3s). SA4s are the largest sub-state regions in the Main Structure of the ASGS and are designed for the output of a variety of regional data, including data from the 2021 Census of Population and Housing.
supersedes_rationale: The domain was inferred from the variable name, and the limitation only restated that the domain was inferred, adding nothing the value definition did not already say.

value_domain: ASGS 2016 Statistical Area Level 4 code
value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Outlet: Physical Address, Statistical Area Level 4 (SA4) Code (ASGS 2016) N(3)', Aristotle item 1511
variable_description: The 2016-vintage SA4 the DSS geocoder assigned to the address. For an outlet DSS defines it as "the designated region representing geographical areas built up from Statistical Areas Level 3 (SA3s) in order to allow for the output of a variety of regional data that a given outlet's physical address is located within, as represented by a code", and the same column on special_client does the same job for the client's residential address. It is stored as a three-character value rather than a number.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Outlet: Physical Address, Statistical Area Level 4 (SA4) Code (ASGS 2016) N(3)', Aristotle item 1511
value_definition: A 3-digit code on the ASGS July 2016 edition: one digit for state or territory then two for the SA4 within it. DSS records that the 2016 edition has 107 SA4 regions, including 18 non-spatial special purpose codes for Migratory, Offshore and Shipping and for No Usual Address in each state, with the Other Territories represented by a single SA4.
limitation: An SA4 is a labour market region, so it tells you which regional labour market an address sits in and nothing about the neighbourhood around it. The 2016 set has one fewer region than the 2021 set and several boundaries were redrawn, so the two SA4 boundary columns on a row will disagree in places where nothing physically moved.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry publishes this exact element for the outlet's physical address, with its definition, its three-character format and comments giving the 2016 region count and the treatment of Other Territories.
evidence_quote: The designated region representing geographical areas built up from Statistical Areas Level 3 (SA3s) in order to allow for the output of a variety of regional data that a given outlet's physical address is located within, as represented by a code.
supersedes_rationale: The domain was 'not specified' with the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, even though DSS publishes a full definition of this element in its own registry.

value_domain: ASGS 2021 Statistical Area Level 4 code
value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, value domain 'Statistical area level 4 (SA4) code (ASGS 2021)', Aristotle item 108924
variable_description: The 2021-vintage SA4 the DSS geocoder assigned to the address, the coarsest boundary code below state. It is the level most Data Exchange output lands on when results have to be published without disclosing a small provider, since each SA4 covers at least about 100,000 residents. On special_outlet it describes the same premises as SA4_ASGS_2021, but the two come from different geocoding paths and are not guaranteed to agree.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, value domain 'Statistical area level 4 (SA4) code (ASGS 2021)', Aristotle item 108924
value_definition: A code for an ASGS Edition 3 SA4 region, of which there are 108. DSS registers its own SA4 (ASGS 2021) domain with a four-character format and a supplementary value of 9 for default, against the three digits ABS uses, so check the stored width before joining to an ABS-coded SA4 column.
limitation: A disagreement between this column and SA4_ASGS_2021 is a geocoding difference, not a boundary change, so taking either as authoritative without checking will quietly move outlets between regions. The column also cannot support labour market analysis of clients, because it locates an address, while an SA4's labour market meaning rests on where people work.
rationale: DSS's metadata registry publishes the ASGS 2021 SA4 value domain it maintains, including its format and default value, and carries the ABS definition of the region. The column's name and its position beside the other DSS-tagged boundary codes place it in that geocoded family.
evidence_quote: Statistical Area Level 4 (SA4s) are geographic areas built from whole Statistical Areas Level 3 (SA3s).
supersedes_rationale: The domain was 'not specified' and the generic no-value-list sentence stood as both the definition and the limitation, with no warning that two differently produced SA4 columns sit on the same table.

value_domain: DEX outcome domain assessment identifier
value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, Client_Assessment (DEX Curated) distribution, data element 'Data Exchange: Outcome domain assessment identifier, ID number', Aristotle item 1709
variable_description: The identifier of one domain rating inside a SCORE assessment, defined by DSS as "a system-generated identifier for a unique outcome domain assessment record in the Data Exchange, represented by a number". A single assessment, identified by ASSESSMENTID, can rate several outcome domains at once, so special_client_assessment holds one row per SCOREID and several SCOREIDs per assessment, each with its own OUTCOMEDOMAIN and OUTCOMEDOMAINSCORE. This is therefore the row key: counting assessments means counting distinct ASSESSMENTID values, not rows.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, Client_Assessment (DEX Curated) distribution, data element 'Data Exchange: Outcome domain assessment identifier, ID number', Aristotle item 1709
value_definition: A system-generated number of up to 19 digits, registered in the curated Data Exchange client assessment table with the format N[N(18)]. It carries no meaning in itself and is not comparable across the client and community assessment tables.
limitation: It identifies a rating, not an outcome. SCOREs are designed to be reported in pairs, an initial rating near the start of service and a subsequent one later, and the pairing is made on the domain across assessments, so one SCOREID on its own shows a level and never a change. Nor does it say who did the rating, which ASSESSEDBY and ASSESSEDBYCODE carry.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry publishes the curated client assessment distribution with this identifier named, defined and given its format, alongside the assessment identifier and the domain and rating columns that show the one-row-per-domain grain.
evidence_quote: A system-generated identifier for a unique outcome domain assessment record in the Data Exchange, represented by a number.
supersedes_rationale: The domain was 'not specified' with the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, and the description was the custodian's line, which left the row grain against ASSESSMENTID unstated.

value_domain: DEX service setting label
value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Session: Service setting, Label', Aristotle item 1331
variable_description: Where or how a session was actually delivered, which DSS defines as "the category of physical location or delivery method for a given session, represented by a label". It is the correction to OUTLETID: the outlet is where staff are based, while this column separates a session held in the office from one at the client's home, a community venue, a partner organisation, a health, education or justice facility, or one delivered by telephone, video or online. For any question about outreach models or about the shift to remote delivery, this is the column that holds the answer.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Session: Service setting, Label', Aristotle item 1331
value_definition: An uppercase label of up to 15 characters. The registry's permissible values, in force from 18 August 2018, are ORGOUTLETOFFICE, CLRES, COMMVENUE, PARORG, TELE, DIGITAL, HEALTHFACILITY, EDUFACILITY and JUSTICEFACILITY; the March 2024 protocols describe Telephone, Video and Online service as three separate settings where the registry carries the single DIGITAL value beside TELE.
limitation: It is optional extended data, so a blank is not an office visit. Only one setting is recorded per session, so a service that began on the phone and finished in person appears as whichever the organisation judged dominant. It also describes the delivery channel, not the client's whereabouts: a telephone session says nothing about where the client was sitting.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry publishes the data element with its definition and full permissible value list, and the protocols give a plain description of each setting category and record the addition of the Video category.
evidence_quote: The category of physical location or delivery method for a given session, represented by a label.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried source-defined values with the boilerplate 'The valid_values field contains the source-defined values' as its definition and 'The source defines the value domain' as its limitation, and never contrasted the setting with the outlet.

value_domain: DEX service type code
value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Session: Service type, Code', Aristotle item 1289
variable_description: The kind of help delivered, defined by DSS as "the main focus of service delivery at a given session, represented by a code". The codes begin at 1 for intake or assessment and 2 for information, advice and referral, and continue through education and skills training, child and youth focused groups, counselling and dispute resolution. Which of them an organisation may use depends on the program activity, because the Data Exchange portal offers only the service types attached to the activity being reported, and special_service_type is the lookup that gives each code its name.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Session: Service type, Code', Aristotle item 1289
value_definition: A number of up to three digits from a single registry-wide list dating from 20 June 2014. The list is long, and the subset available for any one program activity is published in that program's guidance rather than in the protocols.
limitation: Only one service type is recorded per session, so the column understates what a session contained: counselling that also arranged a referral is recorded as counselling alone, on the protocols' rule that the type taking most of the time or achieving the outcome wins. The codes are shared across programs but the menus are not, so a national count by service type mixes activities that use one code for quite different work.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry publishes the session service type data element with its definition, three-digit format and coded values. The protocols set the rule for choosing among several types and state that the portal restricts the list by program activity.
evidence_quote: The main focus of service delivery at a given session, represented by a code.
supersedes_rationale: The domain was 'not specified' with the generic no-value-list sentence used for both the definition and the limitation, even though the registry publishes a coded list.

value_domain: date
value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Session: Conducted date, DDMMYYYY', Aristotle item 890
variable_description: The date of the session a SCORE assessment relates to, defined by DSS as "the date a given session took place, represented by DDMMYYYY". On the assessment tables it is the anchor for ordering initial and subsequent ratings, and it is the date that decides which reporting period the assessment counts against, unlike SESSIONCREATEDDATE and ASSESSMENTCREATEDDATE, which record when the record was keyed in. CONDUCTEDDATE on special_attendance carries the same fact for attendance rows.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Session: Conducted date, DDMMYYYY', Aristotle item 890
value_definition: A calendar date at day resolution, registered in DDMMYYYY form with no time component. The protocols require session dates to be entered as dd/mm/yyyy.
limitation: The date belongs to the session, not to the assessment, so several ratings, several domains and several clients share one value and it cannot order two assessments made on the same day. DSS notes that since 18 August 2018 the service phase label is no longer the primary means of ordering assessments either. It also dates the rating, never the change in circumstances being rated.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry publishes the session conducted date element with its definition and DDMMYYYY format, and the curated client assessment distribution shows how the assessment record hangs off the session.
evidence_quote: The date a given session took place, represented by DDMMYYYY.
supersedes_rationale: The domain was 'not specified' and the generic no-value-list sentence stood as both value definition and limitation, so nothing warned that the date belongs to the session rather than the assessment.

value_domain: record creation timestamp
value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Client outcome assessment: Created date, DDMMYYYY', Aristotle item 1672, the created-date element registered for this table
variable_description: When the session record was first entered into the Data Exchange, as against SESSIONCONDUCTEDDATE, which is when the session happened. The gap between the two is reporting lag: organisations may enter data at any point in a six-month reporting period and for 30 days after it closes, so a session held in January can be created in August. Use it to judge how current the data was and to spot bulk loads, never to date the service.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Client outcome assessment: Created date, DDMMYYYY', Aristotle item 1672, the created-date element registered for this table
value_definition: A date and time stamped by the system when the record was written. The sibling element on this table, ASSESSMENTCREATEDDATE, is registered as the date a record "was entered into a system" in DDMMYYYY form, so expect day resolution at best from the date part.
limitation: It dates the record, not the event, and it is a system value rather than a service fact: a bulk upload creates thousands of session records within one second, and a system migration can restamp records that describe much older sessions. A long gap from the conducted date is a sign of late reporting, not of a long service.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry publishes the created-date concept for this curated table and defines it as the date a record was entered into a system, which is the domain this column carries. The protocols supply the reporting period and close-off rules that explain how large the lag can be.
evidence_quote: The date a given client outcome assessment was entered into a system, represented by DDMMYYYY.
supersedes_rationale: The domain was 'not specified' and the generic no-value-list sentence appeared as both the definition and the limitation, leaving the crucial contrast with the conducted date unsaid.

value_domain: DEX session identifier
value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Data Exchange: Session identifier, ID number', Aristotle item 1775
variable_description: The key of a single instance of service, which DSS defines as "a system-generated identifier for a unique session record in the Data Exchange, represented by a number". The protocols define a session as an individual episode of service stored within a case, and this is the column that holds the session tables together: special_session has one row per session, special_attendance one row per person present, and the assessment tables hang their SCOREs off the same value. Organisations uploading in bulk supply their own session identifier, and the Data Exchange generates one only when the portal field is left blank.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Data Exchange: Session identifier, ID number', Aristotle item 1775
value_definition: A number of up to 19 digits, registered with the format N[N(18)]. It is unique within the case rather than globally meaningful, and the identifier the provider supplied is limited to 50 characters before the Data Exchange converts it.
limitation: A session is a reporting construct, not a unit of effort: a two-hour group workshop and a five-minute phone call are each one session, so session counts are not workload and ASSISTANCEMINUTES is the column for that. The curated attendance table also writes aggregate rows for unidentified clients using the negative of the session identifier as the attendance key, so naive counts of attendance identifiers within a session can be thrown out by those rows.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry publishes the session identifier data element with its definition and format, and the curated attendance distribution documents the negative-identifier convention used for unidentified client attendance. The protocols define the session concept and the identifier's business rules.
evidence_quote: A system-generated identifier for a unique session record in the Data Exchange, represented by a number.
supersedes_rationale: The domain was 'not specified' with the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, and the custodian's description said nothing about how sessions relate to cases, attendances or assessments.

value_domain: dex_source_system (inferred)
variable_description: A code naming the system a program activity record originated in, distinguishing the department's own grants management system from an external load. The item list gives FOFMS and EXTNL as its examples: FOFMS is the department's online funding management system, described by the Australian National Audit Office as "a software system for grants that tracks financial information and is also intended to link financial information with the terms and conditions of funding agreements". It is a provenance column on the activity reference table, sitting with ACTIVITYID, PROGRAMID and GPSPROGRAMID.
description_source: Australian National Audit Office, Funding for Communities and Community Organisations (on FOFMS), read with the DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024)
value_definition: A short uppercase mnemonic. FOFMS marks an activity defined in the departmental funding management system and EXTNL one loaded from outside it; DSS does not publish the full set against this column, so the domain is open.
limitation: It says where the activity's definition was recorded, not who delivered the service or how it was funded. A migration between departmental systems changes this code for an activity whose funding, provider and clients are unchanged, so it must not be used as a grouping variable for trend analysis or read as a difference in program type.
rationale: The PLIDA description supplies two real values (FOFMS, EXTNL) and the field is a short uppercase mnemonic identifying the DSS system that supplied the activity record. I searched the DEX Protocols v13, the Bulk File Upload Technical Specification (Nov 2025) and the Web Services Technical Specification v1.11 and none of them contains a source-system code list; it is an internal DSS warehouse field, so the two documented values are the whole defensible domain.
supersedes_rationale: The earlier reviewer noted the two examples are not a complete codeframe, which is true, but two real published values are enough for a coarse inferred domain.

value_domain: Activity availability start date
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols
variable_description: When a service activity became available to deliver, not when anybody received it. The Data Exchange models a funded service as an activity with an availability window, and clients attach to it through separate session records, so this is a property of the funding arrangement. Using it as a service start date for a client attributes the whole activity's lifetime to everyone who touched it.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols
limitation: The date belongs to the activity, not to any client, and says nothing about when service was actually delivered. The domain is inferred from the DIL wording; the Data Exchange publishes its protocols but not this field's definition.
rationale: The DIL describes the field as the date a given activity is available for service, on the Data Exchange activity table rather than a client table.
evidence_quote: The date that a given activity is available for service.

value_domain: ASGS 2021 state and territory code
value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Australia and State/Territory
variable_description: The state or territory of the outlet's address as ABS coded it under ASGS Edition 3, and the top of the hierarchy the SA1, SA2 and SA4 columns beside it belong to. ABS records that "in general, the total area of each State and Territory, including their offshore islands, is used for statistical purposes as a separate geographic area in the ASGS". OUTLETSTATE on the same row is the state the organisation typed in, so the two can disagree wherever the entered address was wrong or out of date, and this one follows the geocoded address.
description_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Australia and State/Territory
value_definition: A one-digit code: 1 New South Wales, 2 Victoria, 3 Queensland, 4 South Australia, 5 Western Australia, 6 Tasmania, 7 Northern Territory, 8 Australian Capital Territory and 9 Other Territories. It is also the leading digit of the SA1, SA2 and SA4 codes on the same row, so the three are internally consistent by construction.
limitation: Code 9 is a bundle rather than a place: Jervis Bay Territory and the Christmas Island, Cocos (Keeling) Islands and Norfolk Island territories are one category and cannot be separated. The value also describes the premises, so a national help line run from one office puts all of its sessions in a single jurisdiction, which is a poor basis for comparing service levels between states.
rationale: ABS publishes the state and territory coding structure for ASGS Edition 3, with the one-digit codes and the treatment of Other Territories. The custodian's own description of the column as 'State (number)' confirms it is the numeric ABS code rather than an abbreviation.
evidence_quote: In general, the total area of each State and Territory, including their offshore islands, is used for statistical purposes as a separate geographic area in the ASGS.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the state codeframe with the boilerplate 'The valid_values field contains the source-defined values' as its definition and 'The source defines the value domain' as its limitation, and never distinguished it from the organisation-entered OUTLETSTATE.

value_domain: ASGS 2016 state and territory code
value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS): Volume 1 - Main Structure and Greater Capital City Statistical Areas, July 2016
variable_description: The state or territory the DSS geocoder derived from the address on the record, on the 2016 ASGS boundaries: the client's residence on special_client and the outlet's premises on special_outlet. Of the whole boundary code family this is the one that almost never changes between vintages, which makes it the safest fallback when a finer code failed to resolve. The curated Data Exchange client table carries the 2011, 2016 and 2021 state codes side by side.
description_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS): Volume 1 - Main Structure and Greater Capital City Statistical Areas, July 2016
value_definition: A one-digit code from 1 to 9 on the ASGS July 2016 edition, with 9 covering the Other Territories. It is the leading digit of the SA1, SA2, SA3 and SA4 boundary codes on the same row, so it can be derived from any of them.
limitation: State boundaries barely move, so a row where the 2016 and 2021 state codes differ is evidence of an address edit or a geocoding change rather than of a boundary revision, and treating the pair as a migration signal will produce false moves. For a client, the state is the state of the address recorded, which the protocols allow to be the outlet's address where the client is homeless or at risk.
rationale: ABS published the state and territory coding for the July 2016 ASGS edition the column names, and DSS's curated client distribution lists the 2011, 2016 and 2021 state boundary columns as one geocoded family.
evidence_quote: Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS): Volume 1 - Main Structure and Greater Capital City Statistical Areas, July 2016
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the ABS state codeframe with the boilerplate definition and the generic 'The source defines the value domain' limitation, saying nothing about the vintage pairing or the address substitution rules.

value_domain: ASGS 2021 state and territory code
value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Australia and State/Territory
variable_description: The state or territory of the address on ASGS Edition 3 boundaries, assigned by the DSS geocoder to the client record and to the outlet record. It is the coarsest of the 2021 boundary codes and the one most Data Exchange program reporting is broken down by, because activities are commissioned jurisdiction by jurisdiction. On special_outlet it should agree with STATE_ASGS_2021, which ABS derived independently through the address register match.
description_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Australia and State/Territory
value_definition: A one-digit code from 1 to 9 under ASGS Edition 3, July 2021 to June 2026, where 9 is Other Territories. Australia itself is coded AUS in Edition 3, replacing the numeric 036 used in the 2016 edition.

DSS is a Commonwealth department, several Data Exchange program values belong to state agencies, and a client's state and the funding jurisdiction are separate questions. Nor is it a reliable statement of usual residence: a client can move between service episodes without the address on their record being updated.
rationale: ABS publishes the state and territory codes and the Other Territories treatment for the edition named in the column. DSS's curated client distribution lists this column with the rest of the 2021 boundary set produced by its geocoder.
evidence_quote: States and Territories are identified by unique one-digit codes
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the ABS state codeframe with the boilerplate definition and the generic limitation, and gave no indication that the same fact appears twice on special_outlet from two different geocoding paths.

value_domain: PLIDA agency person identifier (anonymised)
value_source: ABS, Person Level Integrated Data Asset (PLIDA)
variable_description: The person key that runs through the Data Exchange tables: one client carries the same value across special_client, special_attendance, special_client_assessment, special_client_disability and special_community_assessment, which is what turns scattered session rows into a service history. It is the DSS client identifier in anonymised form, not a PLIDA-wide person number: ABS links datasets through a "Person Linkage Spine" held "separate from the main body of data", so joining a Data Exchange client to their Medicare, tax or payment records means going out through the agency spine file to the spine identifier and back in through another agency's identifier.
description_source: ABS, Person Level Integrated Data Asset (PLIDA)
value_definition: An opaque identifier with no internal structure and no decodable content. It is stable within the DSS extract and meaningless outside it, so it can be compared for equality and nothing else.
limitation: It identifies a client record, not a person. The Data Exchange creates client records at the delivery organisation level, so someone who registers with two providers under different details can hold two identifiers until the statistical linkage key brings them together. Linkage to the PLIDA spine also fails for a share of records, and an unlinked client is missing from the other datasets rather than absent from them.
rationale: ABS documents the Person Linkage Spine as the mechanism by which agency datasets are linked, held separately from the data itself, which is why each agency's records carry their own anonymised person identifier rather than a shared one. The curated Data Exchange client distribution shows client records are held against a delivery organisation, which is what makes duplicate client records possible.
evidence_quote: The Person Linkage Spine allows us to link datasets through a spine of key information, separate from the main body of data.
supersedes_rationale: The domain was guessed from the variable name as an opaque identifier, and the limitation only restated that the domain was inferred and open, which told a reader nothing about how to join the column or where linkage fails.

value_domain: system-versioning period end timestamp
value_source: Microsoft, SQL Server temporal tables documentation, which defines the SysStartTime and SysEndTime period columns this pair follows
variable_description: The moment this version of the row stopped being the current one. The seven reference tables that carry it — activity, client, client disability, organisation, outlet, program and service type — are delivered as full row histories rather than snapshots, and SYSSTARTTIME and SYSENDTIME bound the window in which each version was live. The current version carries the maximum value the type allows rather than a null, so the filter for a snapshot is SYSENDTIME at its maximum, or equivalently CURRENTRECORD set to 1.
description_source: Microsoft, SQL Server temporal tables documentation, which defines the SysStartTime and SysEndTime period columns this pair follows
value_definition: A datetime in UTC closing a version's period. Following the system-versioned temporal table convention the columns are named for, the open row is given 9999-12-31 23:59:59.9999999 rather than a null, so comparisons against a null will silently drop the current record.
limitation: It records when the database row was superseded, not when the thing it describes ended: an outlet that closed in March but was edited in September ends its version in September. ENDDATE on special_activity is the service fact — the date an activity is no longer available for service — while this column is only the record's lifetime in the system.
rationale: The column names, the accompanying CURRENTRECORD flag and RECORDSEQNBR counter, and the presence of SysStartTime and SysEndTime in DSS's own curated Data Exchange client table all match the system-versioned temporal table pattern, whose period column semantics and open-row sentinel value are published by Microsoft. The specific values DSS stores are not published, hence medium confidence.
supersedes_rationale: The domain was 'not specified' with the generic no-value-list sentence as both the definition and the limitation, so nothing told a reader that failing to filter this column multiplies every entity by its version count.

value_domain: system-versioning period start timestamp
value_source: Microsoft, SQL Server temporal tables documentation, which defines the SysStartTime and SysEndTime period columns this pair follows
variable_description: The moment this version of the row became current. Reading any of the seven reference tables without filtering on it counts one outlet, client or activity several times over, because the product ships every version of every reference record rather than a snapshot. Paired with SYSENDTIME it gives the window in which the row was live, and RECORDSEQNBR numbers the same versions in the same order. A record that has never been edited has one version, whose start time is when it was first written.
description_source: Microsoft, SQL Server temporal tables documentation, which defines the SysStartTime and SysEndTime period columns this pair follows
value_definition: A datetime in UTC opening the period during which this version was current. Under the system-versioned convention the columns are named for, one version's end time equals the next version's start time, so the periods abut exactly and leave no gaps in an entity's history.
limitation: It is a database write time, so it dates the data entry rather than the event: a client record created in 2019 that describes services from 2016 carries a 2019 start time. It also cannot be read across tables as a measure of when anything happened, because a bulk load stamps thousands of unrelated rows with a single time.
rationale: The pairing with SYSENDTIME, the CURRENTRECORD flag and RECORDSEQNBR, together with DSS listing SysStartTime and SysEndTime in its own curated Data Exchange client table, identify these as system-versioned period columns, whose semantics Microsoft publishes. DSS does not publish the stored values, hence medium confidence.
supersedes_rationale: The domain was 'not specified', the generic no-value-list sentence was printed as both definition and limitation, and the description was the custodian's five words, 'Record start date and time'.

value_domain: calendar date
value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols, Version 11, March 2024, sections 3.4 and 10.3
variable_description: The calendar date a Data Exchange calendar-table row stands for. Every other column on the row is derived from it: THEDAY, THEDAYNAME, THEDAYOFWEEK, THEWEEK, THEISOWEEK, THEMONTH, THEQUARTER, THEYEAR and THEFINANCIALYEAR, with THEREPORTINGPERIOD and REPORTINGPERIODENDTIME placing it in one of the two six-monthly reporting periods. It exists so a session's conducted date can be joined to consistent period labels rather than each analyst deriving their own, which matters because the protocols count a session against a reporting period by its date.
description_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols, Version 11, March 2024, sections 3.4 and 10.3
value_definition: A calendar date at day resolution and the primary key of special_ref_calendar, with one row for every day the table spans, weekends and public holidays included.
limitation: The table describes the calendar, not the data: a date is present whether or not any session occurred on it, so counting rows here measures the span of the calendar and never activity. Joining to it cannot fill gaps either — a day with no sessions simply produces no match on the other side of the join.
rationale: The protocols set the counting rule that a session belongs to the reporting period its date falls in, and define the two six-monthly periods, which is what this date dimension exists to implement. The registry's own column list for special_ref_calendar shows the derived date parts that hang off this key.
evidence_quote: A session is counted against a reporting period if the date of the session fell within the reporting period and at least one client is attached.
supersedes_rationale: The domain was 'not specified', the generic no-value-list sentence stood as both definition and limitation, and the description was the custodian's catch-all 'Calendar related data fields', shared with fourteen other columns in the table.

description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 3.4 counting rules for clients, cases and sessions

The column-level reading is inferred from the sibling columns in special_ref_calendar, which are the standard parts of a warehouse date dimension (THEDATE, THEDAYNAME, THEDAYOFWEEK, THEDAYOFYEAR, THEWEEK, THEISOWEEK, THEMONTH, THEMONTHNAME, THEQUARTER, THEYEAR), and no DSS document defines the warehouse column itself.

description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 3.4 counting rules for clients, cases and sessions

value_domain: day of week index, 1-7 (inferred)
variable_description: The weekday index of a calendar date in the DEX date reference table. The table is a calendar dimension: one row per date, carrying THEDATE, THEDAYNAME, THEMONTH, THEQUARTER, THEFINANCIALYEAR, THEISOWEEK and THEREPORTINGPERIOD, so that session and case dates can be rolled up to any of those periods. This column exists to let sessions be counted by day of week, which is how weekend and after-hours service delivery is identified.
description_source: PLIDA DEX data item list, read with the DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024) on reporting periods
value_definition: An integer from 1 to 7 indexing the day within the week. THEDAYNAME on the same row carries the corresponding name in words, and THEDAYOFYEAR gives the ordinal position within the year.
limitation: DSS does not publish which day is 1, and the value can follow either a Monday-first or a Sunday-first convention depending on the database setting used to build the table, so the index must be read against THEDAYNAME before any weekday or weekend split is derived from it. The table is also a full calendar, so a date appearing here implies nothing about whether any service was delivered on it.
rationale: The field sits in the DEX calendar dimension table special_ref_calendar alongside THEDAY, THEDAYNAME, THEDAYOFYEAR, THEWEEK, THEISOWEEK, THEMONTH and THEMONTHNAME; with a separate THEDAYNAME holding the weekday label, THEDAYOFWEEK is the numeric weekday index taking 1 to 7. value_domain: day of year, 1 to 366
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 3.4 counting rules for clients, cases and sessions
variable_description: The position of the date within its calendar year, counting 1 January as day one. On the Data Exchange calendar it is the attribute that lets service volumes be lined up across years without month boundaries getting in the way, which is how seasonal demand for emergency relief or financial counselling is usually looked at. It is a property of the date alone and repeats identically for every year in the table.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 3.4 counting rules for clients, cases and sessions

rationale: The Data Exchange Protocols establish the date-driven counting the calendar table supports. The 1 to 366 domain is inferred from the column name and from the sibling calendar columns; no DSS document defines the warehouse column.

value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 3.4 counting rules for clients, cases and sessions

evidence_quote: A session is counted against a reporting period if the date of the session fell within the reporting period and at least one client is attached.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the table-wide description 'Calendar related data fields' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice, which left the ISO week indistinguishable from THEWEEK.

The Protocols add the counting rule: a session belongs to a period if the session date fell inside it and at least one client is attached.

value_definition: A six-month period label covering either 1 July to 31 December or 1 January to 30 June. REPORTINGPERIODENDTIME on the same calendar row carries the closing date of that period.
limitation: The period says when a service is counted, not when it was recorded: organisations may enter data at any time during the period and for 30 days after it closes, and later still if the department grants a system re-opening, so this is not a measure of data currency. A case with sessions in both halves of the year is counted in both periods, so summing counts by period double counts continuing clients and cases.
rationale: The Quick Start Guide states the two periods and the 30 day close-off directly, and the Protocols give the counting rule that attaches a session, case or client to a period. Both are published by the Department of Social Services, which runs the collection.
evidence_quote: There are two reporting periods per year which run from 1 July to 31 December and 1 January to 30 June, with a 30 day close off period to allow you to finalise your data.
supersedes_rationale: The entry gave the custodian's line, 'The Reporting Period in which a session was conducted', which never said how long a period is or when it starts, and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation.

value_domain: week of year number
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 3.4 counting rules for clients, cases and sessions
variable_description: The week of the year this row's date falls in, numbered on the warehouse's own rule rather than the ISO rule. It exists alongside THEISOWEEK precisely because the two differ: a calendar table carries both so that a report can pick the convention it needs. Joined to the session tables it supports weekly delivery counts within a reporting period.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 3.4 counting rules for clients, cases and sessions
value_definition: A week number within the calendar year, running from 1 to 53 or 54 depending on where the year starts in the week.
limitation: The rule for the first and last weeks of the year is not published, so a week 1 may be a part week of one or two days and week counts are not comparable across years. Values here also cannot be matched to the ISO week numbers in THEISOWEEK, which start weeks on Monday and place week 1 differently.
rationale: The Data Exchange Protocols establish the date-driven counting the calendar table serves. That this column is a non-ISO week number is inferred from THEISOWEEK existing separately on the same row; no DSS document states the numbering rule.
evidence_quote: A session is counted against a reporting period if the date of the session fell within the reporting period and at least one client is attached.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the table-wide description 'Calendar related data fields' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice, which left this column and THEISOWEEK looking interchangeable.

value_domain: calendar year
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 10.3 reporting periods and deadlines
variable_description: The calendar year of this row's date on the Data Exchange calendar. It is the coarsest level of the calendar hierarchy and the one most often joined to sessions for an annual series, but it is the January-to-December year, not the funding year the collection is built around. THEFINANCIALYEAR on the same row holds the July-to-June year, and THEREPORTINGPERIOD holds the six-month half.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 10.3 reporting periods and deadlines
value_definition: A four-digit Gregorian year taken from the date in THEDATE on the same row.
limitation: An annual count grouped on this column will not match any published Data Exchange or departmental figure, because those run from July to June; each calendar year mixes the second half of one funding year with the first half of the next. It also cannot be combined with THEISOWEEK without splitting the week that spans the year end.
rationale: The Data Exchange Protocols set out the two six-month reporting periods, which is what makes the calendar year the wrong unit for reconciling with published output. The four-digit year reading is inferred from the column name and the date-dimension shape of special_ref_calendar.
evidence_quote: The Data Exchange has two standardised six monthly performance reporting periods each year:
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the table-wide description 'Calendar related data fields' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice.

value_domain: National Disability Advocacy Program session topic
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 5.3.4 and Table 14, National Disability Advocacy Program session level data
variable_description: The advocacy issue a National Disability Advocacy Program session was about, recorded on the session record. The Protocols describe the item as captured at the session level, where "This field allows organisations to select the reason why a client is accessing a service", and make it mandatory only for that program. The published list is of advocacy issues rather than service types: abuse, neglect and violence, discrimination and rights, NDIS access and planning, housing and homelessness, legal access to justice, transport, and about a dozen more. It sits beside SERVICETYPEID, which records what was delivered, while this records what it was about.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 5.3.4 and Table 14, National Disability Advocacy Program session level data
value_definition: One label from a closed list of about twenty advocacy issues published in Table 14 of the Protocols. Despite the column name the stored value is the label text, not a number.
limitation: Only one topic is recorded per session, so a session that dealt with a housing problem and a payment problem shows one of them and the other is invisible. The field is collected only for National Disability Advocacy Program activities, so an empty value almost always means a different program rather than an unknown reason, and it must not be read as a diagnosis, a disability type or an outcome.
rationale: The Protocols name the item, place it at session level, restrict it to the National Disability Advocacy Program and publish its full list of values in Table 14.
evidence_quote: Topic: this item is captured at the session level. This field allows organisations to select the reason why a client is accessing a service.
supersedes_rationale: The entry restated the custodian's line about the reason a client is accessing a service without saying that only one program collects it or what the topics are, and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice.

value_domain: education and skills training domain flag
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 6.2 reasons for seeking assistance and section 6.4 referrals to other services
variable_description: A marker that education and skills training was one of the domains recorded for a client, set on two different reference tables. On the reasons-for-assistance table it flags the reason category the Protocols define as "Education and skills training: where the client is seeking to engage with education and skills training to improve their independence, participation and wellbeing"; on the referral table it flags a referral made for that purpose. The columns beside it, HOUSING, EMPLOYMENT, MENTAL, MONEY, PERSONAL and the rest, are the other domains from the same list, and several can be set on one row because a client can present with more than one need.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 6.2 reasons for seeking assistance and section 6.4 referrals to other services
value_definition: A yes-or-no indicator rather than a code, one column per domain on a reference row keyed by ASSISTANCENEEDEDKEY or REFERRALTOKEY. The domain list is the standard set of SCORE circumstance domains used across the Data Exchange.
limitation: The flag records a presenting need or the purpose of a referral, not anything delivered or achieved: a referral flag means a referral was made, not that the client took it up or got help. Reporting the reason is optional and, as the Protocols note, the real reason often only emerges after a client engages, so an unset flag is not evidence that a client had no training need.
rationale: The Protocols define the eleven reason-for-assistance categories and the matching referral purposes, and this column and its neighbours reproduce that list one column per category, including the CARING and OTHER columns that appear only on the referral table.
evidence_quote: Education and skills training: where the client is seeking to engage with education and skills training to improve their independence, participation and wellbeing.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Seeking assistance related to skills training', which did not say it was a flag, did not name the classification behind it and did not mention the second table where it means a referral purpose, and it repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice.

value_domain: count of unidentified attendees at a session
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), sections 2.6 and 5.2.2, and Table 9 priority requirements session level data
variable_description: How many people attended a session without a client record being created for them. The Protocols define the item as "the aggregate number of unidentified clients who attended a session" and say it "should be limited to large groups where the collection of client level information is not feasible", which in practice means public events, information sessions and community outreach. These attendances are the only trace those people leave: they have no client row, no demographics and no person identifier, so nothing about them can be linked to the PLIDA spine.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), sections 2.6 and 5.2.2, and Table 9 priority requirements session level data
value_definition: A count of people on the session record, defaulting to zero, entered as a number up to 999, and constrained so that it cannot exceed the case-level figure carried in UNIDENTIFIEDCLIENTCASEMAX.
limitation: The number counts attendances at one session, not people: someone who comes to three sessions is counted three times, and the file gives no way to tell repeat attendance from new attendance. It also carries no age, sex, Indigenous status or cultural and linguistic background, so an event's audience cannot be described at all. Any person-level analysis of the Data Exchange silently drops these people while service-level counts keep them, which is the usual source of a mismatch between the two.
rationale: The Protocols define the session-level item, give its purpose, and specify the field as a number with a default of zero and a maximum of 999 that cannot exceed the case-level value.
evidence_quote: Unidentified client attendance: the aggregate number of unidentified clients who attended a session. This should be limited to large groups where the collection of client level information is not feasible.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'The number of unidentified clients for the session', which did not explain who these people are, why they are counted this way or that they cannot be linked, and it repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice.

value_domain: case-level count of unidentified clients
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), sections 2.6 and 5.2.2, and Table 8 priority requirements case level data
variable_description: The case-level number of unidentified clients, carried onto the session row as the ceiling that session attendance sits under. The Protocols explain the split: case-level numbers "estimate the total number of unidentified clients who are anticipated to attend services", the session-level number "records how many unidentified clients actually attended that instance of service", and this "prevents double counting". Their worked example is a case with two sessions of 100 unidentified clients each, which means up to 100 distinct people, not 200. Reading it beside UNIDENTIFIEDCLIENTATTENDANCE on the same row is how the two are meant to be used.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), sections 2.6 and 5.2.2, and Table 8 priority requirements case level data
value_definition: A count of people attached to the case rather than to the session, entered as a number up to 999, and repeated on every session record belonging to that case.
limitation: It is an expected ceiling rather than a measured headcount, so it cannot be used as a number of clients served, and adding it up across the sessions of a case counts the same group over and over. It also gives no way to tell how many of the unidentified people at different sessions of a case were the same people, so the true number of distinct attendees lies somewhere between the largest single session and this cap.
rationale: The Protocols set out the case and session split for unidentified clients, state that the case figure is an anticipated total, and give the rule that session attendance must be less than or equal to it.
evidence_quote: Unidentified client numbers captured at the case level estimate the total number of unidentified clients who are anticipated to attend services.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only that it was the total number of unidentified clients across sessions in a case, which reads as a headcount rather than a cap, and it repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice.

value_domain: record update timestamp
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), sections 3.5 outlets, 5.2 priority requirements and 10.3 reporting deadlines
variable_description: When the Data Exchange system last changed this record, not when anything happened to a client. It sits on the reference tables that describe the service system rather than the service itself, including activity, program, service type, organisation, outlet, client and client disability, always beside CREATEDDATETIME and, on the activity table, beside CURRENTRECORD, RECORDSEQNBR, SYSSTARTTIME and SYSENDTIME, which together hold the record's version history. Use it to work out which version of a reference record you are reading, and use the session date for anything about service delivery.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), sections 3.5 outlets, 5.2 priority requirements and 10.3 reporting deadlines
value_definition: A timestamp with both a date and a time of day, written by the source system when the row was amended, rather than a date reported by the funded organisation.
limitation: The timestamp belongs to the row, not to the thing described: an outlet record updated in 2023 is not evidence the outlet changed in 2023, and the sessions already delivered there are unaffected. It also does not say what changed, so a corrected spelling and a genuine change to a program's end date look identical, and a record never amended keeps a stale value that is easily mistaken for evidence of currency.
rationale: The Protocols describe the entities these tables hold, activities, programs, outlets, organisations and clients, and the reporting cycle that governs when data is entered, but they document what organisations report rather than warehouse audit fields. The audit reading is inferred from the column pairing with CREATEDDATETIME and from the version-history columns on the activity table.
evidence_quote: Organisations can enter data at any time within a reporting period, and are encouraged to do so regularly to make best use of the self-service reports and avoid unnecessary backlog or 'crunch' periods.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'The date and time that a given activity record was updated', which named the field without warning that it dates the record and not the service, and it repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice.

value_domain: Date (YYYY-MM-DD)
value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution CCD_HCC_EXT (PLIDA), column action_date
variable_description: The day Centrelink processed the concession card decision that this row records. DSS defines the column as "The date on which a concession card is actioned, expressed as YYYY-MM-DD", which makes it a processing date rather than an entitlement date: CARD_ISSUE_DATE is when the card was produced and CARD_START_DATE is when it could first be used. All four concession card tables carry it, so a card's administrative sequence of action, issue, start and expiry reads the same way for a health care card, a pensioner card, a low income card and a seniors health card.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution CCD_HCC_EXT (PLIDA), column action_date
value_definition: A calendar date written YYYY-MM-DD. The domain is open: any date on which Centrelink actioned a card record, which in DOMINO runs from 2000 to the extract date.
limitation: It does not say what the action was. A grant, a reissue after loss, a variation and a cancellation all stamp this one field, so REASON_CODE and END_REASON_CODE are needed to tell them apart. An action date can also fall either side of the card's own start date, so it cannot stand in for the date entitlement began.
rationale: The DSS Aristotle registry publishes the PLIDA distribution of the health care card table and gives a verbatim definition for the action_date column, alongside the sibling date columns that distinguish it.
evidence_quote: The date on which a concession card is actioned, expressed as YYYY-MM-DD.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's wording, 'Concession card action date', with the generic sentence 'The source metadata does not publish a finite value list.' printed as both the value definition and the limitation, so it never said which of the four card dates this one is.

value_domain: domino_activity_participant_code
values: ["Y: Yes","N: No","NR: Not required","(blank): Missing (supplementary)"]
value_source: DSS Aristotle Metadata Registry, data element "Recipient: Activity participant, Code" (item 54207), bound to the DOMINO (External PLIDA Version) distribution column
variable_description: A flag on a medical or capacity assessment record for whether activity participation requirements applied to the recipient. DSS defines the element as "Indicator of activity participant requirements for a medical assessment", which places it on the assessment rather than on the payment. It sits in the medical conditions detail table with the impairment code and rating, the assessed work capacity and the incapacity period dates, so it qualifies how the assessment was conducted rather than what the person was entitled to.
description_source: DSS Aristotle Metadata Registry, data element "Recipient: Activity participant, Code" (item 54207)
value_definition: Three permissible codes — Y for yes, N for no and NR for not required — with a blank as the supplementary missing value. The domain is the DSS permissible value list for the element and carries no other codes.
limitation: It records whether requirements applied, not what the person did. The code says nothing about whether an activity was undertaken, attended, exempted or breached, and it carries neither the hours nor the type of activity. Nor does an NR mean the recipient was excused from mutual obligations generally; it means participation requirements were not relevant to this particular assessment.
rationale: The PLIDA MCD_DTLS_EXT distribution binds mcd_dtls.actv_prtcpn_code to this DSS data element, which publishes a Yes/No/Not required domain.
evidence_quote: Y Yes | N No | NR Not required
supersedes_rationale: The earlier pass did not find the DSS Aristotle data element page, which does publish the codeframe.

value_domain: domino_address_priority_code
values: ["1: Temporary","2: Term","3: Home","5: Postal/Other"]
value_source: DSS Aristotle Metadata Registry, data element "Address: Address priority, Code" (item 54356), bound to the DOMINO (External PLIDA Version) distribution column
variable_description: Which of a recipient's concurrently held addresses should be treated as their location on a given day. DSS defines it as a "Derived code highlighting address priority for identifying the location of a recipient on a given day", so it is a tie-breaking rule rather than an observation. On the derived location table it explains why one address episode survived into the geography columns beside it — ARID_HASH_TRUNC, the meshblock and the 2021 ASGS areas — when the person had several addresses recorded at once.
description_source: DSS Aristotle Metadata Registry, data element "Address: Address priority, Code" (item 54356)
value_definition: A single digit ranking the address types: 1 temporary, 2 term, 3 home, 5 postal or other. The published list has no value 4, and lower numbers take precedence when several address records overlap in time.
limitation: It is a rule for choosing between addresses, not evidence about any one of them. A row carrying priority 3 does not mean the person had no term or postal address, only that the home address won on that day, and the priority says nothing about how long the address was held or how reliable it is — START_DATE and END_DATE carry the duration.
rationale: LOC_DERIVED, LOC_DTLS_EXT and LOC_POS_TEMP_TERM_DTLS_EXT all bind addr_prty to this DSS data element, which publishes a four-value priority scale.
evidence_quote: 1 Temporary | 2 Term | 3 Home
supersedes_rationale: A public DOMINO code table does exist: the DSS Aristotle registry publishes the 1/2/3/5 priority scale.

value_domain: domino_address_type_code
values: ["BUS: Business Address","FPO: FAO Postal Address","HOM: Home Address","NAD: Nominee Address","PHY: Physical Address","POS: Postal Address","TEM: Temporary Address","TER: Term Address"]
value_source: DSS Aristotle Metadata Registry, data element "Address: Address type, Code" (item 369), bound to the DOMINO (External PLIDA Version) distribution column
variable_description: What kind of address the recipient supplied on this address detail record — home, postal, temporary, term, business or a nominee's. DSS defines the element as "The type of address given by a recipient". In the address detail table it qualifies POSTCODE, STATE, MESHBLOCK, SA1_MAINCODE and SA2_MAINCODE on the same row, so it decides whether that geography describes where the person lives or only where their mail arrives.
description_source: DSS Aristotle Metadata Registry, data element "Address: Address type, Code" (item 369)
value_definition: Eight three-letter codes: BUS business, FPO FAO postal, HOM home, NAD nominee, PHY physical, POS postal, TEM temporary and TER term address. The list is the DSS permissible value set for the element.
limitation: A home address type is not proof of residence at the coded meshblock. Nominee and FAO postal addresses belong to a person acting for the recipient, and a business or postal address can be a workplace or a post office, so residential analysis has to filter to HOM or PHY first. MESHMATCH on the same row separately records whether the meshblock came from the address text or from coordinates.
rationale: LOC_DTLS_EXT and LOC_POS_TEMP_TERM_DTLS_EXT bind addr_type_code to the DSS Address type code element with eight published codes.
evidence_quote: BUS Business Address | FPO FAO Postal Address | HOM Home Address
supersedes_rationale: The DSS Aristotle registry publishes the address type code table the earlier pass could not find.

value_domain: domino_address_type_code
value_source: DSS Aristotle Metadata Registry, data element "Address: Address type, Code" (item 369), bound to the DOMINO (External PLIDA Version) distribution column
variable_description: The address type carried on the derived location history, the table that gives a recipient one chosen address per period. DSS defines the underlying element as "The type of address given by a recipient". Unlike ADDR_TYPE_CODE in the address detail table, this column describes the address DSS selected for the episode, so it sits with START_DATE, END_DATE, ARID_HASH_TRUNC and the 2021 ASGS geography; POSTALTYPE beside it splits postal addresses further.
description_source: DSS Aristotle Metadata Registry, data element "Address: Address type, Code" (item 369), bound to the DOMINO derived location table
value_definition: The same DSS address type domain as ADDR_TYPE_CODE, whose three-letter codes include HOM, POS, TEM and TER, although the PLIDA item list publishes no value list against this particular column.
limitation: It is not a second, independent observation of the address type. The derived table keeps one address per date range after ADDR_PRTY has been applied, so a type that lost the priority contest never appears here at all. Counting address types in the derived table therefore under-counts the addresses a person actually held, and a person can look like they never had a postal address when they always did.
rationale: The LOC_DERIVED (PLIDA) distribution binds loc_derived.adr_typ to the same DSS Address type code element.
evidence_quote: BUS Business Address | FPO FAO Postal Address | HOM Home Address
supersedes_rationale: The DSS Aristotle registry publishes the address type code table the earlier pass could not find.

value_domain: Age in completed years
value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distributions SNAP_DOMINO_BETA_EXT (PLIDA, item 110613) and STATIC_DEMOGS (PLIDA, item 84485)
variable_description: A recipient's age in completed years, fixed at a reference date rather than measured at the event on the row. Which reference date depends on the table: STATIC_DEMOGS gives "The age of a person as of the extract date", while Snap-DOMINO gives "The age of a person as of the snap date", the day carried in SNAP_DATE. Age at a payment, a card or an assessment therefore has to be worked out from YEAR_OF_BIRTH and MONTH_OF_BIRTH against that event's own dates.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distributions SNAP_DOMINO_BETA_EXT (PLIDA, item 110613) and STATIC_DEMOGS (PLIDA, item 84485)
value_definition: Whole years, format N{NN} on the snapshot distribution, so a two- or three-digit integer with no fractional part and no code list.
limitation: It is not age at the event. Joining STATIC_DEMOGS to a payment history record and reading AGE gives the person's age at extraction, which can be many years after the payment, so an 'age at first payment' built this way is wrong by the length of the person's history. The two tables also disagree with each other by design, since one is anchored to the extract and the other to the snapshot day.
rationale: The registry publishes both PLIDA distributions and gives a different reference date for the same column name in each, which is the fact a user needs and the fplida description omitted.
evidence_quote: The age of a person as of the snap date.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Recipient age as of extract date' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and the description was wrong for the Snap-DOMINO occurrence, where age is measured at the snap date.

value_domain: domino_snap_age_group
values: ["Under 16: under 16","21 to 24: 21 to 24","25 to 34: 25 to 34","35 to 44: 35 to 44","45 to 54: 45 to 54","55 to 64: 55 to 64","65 and over: 65 and over","Unknown: Unknown (supplementary)"]
value_source: DSS Aristotle Metadata Registry, data element "Person: Age group" (item 109634), bound to the DOMINO (External PLIDA Version) distribution column; the published band list runs Under 16 then 21 to 24 upward, with no 16-20 band shown on the page
variable_description: The recipient's age band on the Snap-DOMINO snapshot date, given as a band rather than a number of years. DSS defines the element as "A code set representing chronological groupings of age of a person". It sits on the point-in-time snapshot table beside AGE, the concession card flags and SNAP_DATE, so it answers what the age profile of the payment population looked like on a chosen day rather than at any event.
description_source: DSS Aristotle Metadata Registry, data element "Person: Age group" (item 109634)
value_definition: Text band labels rather than numeric codes: Under 16, then 21 to 24, 25 to 34, 35 to 44, 45 to 54, 55 to 64 and 65 and over, with Unknown as a supplementary value. The bands are the DSS permissible values for the element.

No band covers ages 16 to 20, so a count by AGE_GROUP will not sum to the snapshot population and the missing young people are not in Unknown either; use AGE on the same table where a full distribution is needed. The bands are also unequal in width, so a rate calculated per band is not comparable between bands without standardising.
rationale: SNAP_DOMINO_BETA_EXT binds age_group to the DSS "Person: Age group" element, whose Snap age group value domain lists the released bands verbatim.
